# REAL-WORLD USE CASE: E-COMMERCE ORDER PROCESSING
# ============================================================================
def ecommerce_use_case():
    """
    Real-world example: E-commerce order processing with multiple lookups
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("REAL-WORLD USE CASE: E-COMMERCE ORDER PROCESSING")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Create realistic e-commerce data
    
    # 1. Orders (Fact Table - Large)
    orders = spark.createDataFrame([
        (1001, 501, "2024-01-15 10:30:00", "completed", 150.00),
        (1002, 502, "2024-01-15 11:45:00", "completed", 320.00),
        (1003, 503, "2024-01-15 14:20:00", "pending", 89.99),
        (1004, 501, "2024-01-16 09:15:00", "completed", 450.00),
        (1005, 504, "2024-01-16 16:30:00", "cancelled", 200.00),
    ], ["order_id", "customer_id", "order_date", "status", "total_amount"])
    
    # 2. Customers (Dimension - Small, broadcast candidate)
    customers = spark.createDataFrame([
        (501, "Alice Johnson", "alice@email.com", "Premium", "USA"),
        (502, "Bob Smith", "bob@email.com", "Standard", "UK"),
        (503, "Carol White", "carol@email.com", "Premium", "Canada"),
        (504, "David Brown", "david@email.com", "Basic", "USA"),
    ], ["customer_id", "customer_name", "email", "membership", "country"])
    
    # 3. Order Items (Fact Detail Table)
    order_items = spark.createDataFrame([
        (1, 1001, "PROD001", 2, 50.00),
        (2, 1001, "PROD002", 1, 50.00),
        (3, 1002, "PROD003", 1, 320.00),
        (4, 1003, "PROD001", 1, 50.00),
        (5, 1003, "PROD004", 1, 39.99),
        (6, 1004, "PROD002", 3, 150.00),
    ], ["item_id", "order_id", "product_id", "quantity", "item_total"])
    
    # 4. Products (Dimension - Small, broadcast candidate)
    products = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("PROD001", "Wireless Mouse", "Electronics", 25.00, 100),
        ("PROD002", "USB Cable", "Electronics", 15.00, 200),
        ("PROD003", "Laptop Stand", "Accessories", 320.00, 50),
        ("PROD004", "Mousepad", "Accessories", 12.99, 150),
    ], ["product_id", "product_name", "category", "unit_price", "stock"])
    
    # 5. Shipping Zones (Dimension - Very Small, broadcast)
    shipping_zones = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("USA", "Zone1", 5.00, 2),
        ("UK", "Zone2", 15.00, 5),
        ("Canada", "Zone2", 12.00, 4),
    ], ["country", "zone", "shipping_cost", "delivery_days"])
    
    # 6. Discount Rules (Dimension - Small, broadcast)
    discount_rules = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("Premium", 0.15),
        ("Standard", 0.10),
        ("Basic", 0.05),
    ], ["membership", "discount_rate"])
    
    print("\n--- Step 1: Enrich Orders with Customer Info (Broadcast Lookup) ---")
    
    # Use broadcast for small dimension tables
    orders_enriched = orders.join(
        broadcast(customers),
        "customer_id",
        "left"
    )
    
    orders_enriched.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Step 2: Add Order Items with Product Details (Multiple Broadcasts) ---")
    
    # Chain multiple broadcast lookups
    order_details = order_items \
        .join(broadcast(products), "product_id", "left") \
        .join(orders_enriched, "order_id", "left")
    
    order_details.select(
        "order_id",
        "customer_name",
        "product_name",
        "quantity",
        "unit_price",
        "item_total"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Step 3: Calculate Discounts (Hash Lookup Pattern) ---")
    
    # Create discount lookup map
    discount_map = {
        row['membership']: row['discount_rate'] 
        for row in discount_rules.collect()
    }
    broadcast_discounts = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(discount_map)
    
    # Apply discount using UDF
    @udf(DoubleType())
    def calculate_discount(membership, amount):
        discount_rate = broadcast_discounts.value.get(membership, 0.0)
        return amount * discount_rate
    
    orders_with_discount = orders_enriched.withColumn(
        "discount_amount",
        calculate_discount(col("membership"), col("total_amount"))
    ).withColumn(
        "amount_after_discount",
        col("total_amount") - col("discount_amount")
    )
    
    orders_with_discount.select(
        "order_id",
        "customer_name",
        "membership",
        "total_amount",
        "discount_amount",
        "amount_after_discount"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Step 4: Add Shipping Costs (Broadcast Lookup) ---")
    
    final_orders = orders_with_discount.join(
        broadcast(shipping_zones),
        "country",
        "left"
    ).withColumn(
        "final_total",
        col("amount_after_discount") + coalesce(col("shipping_cost"), lit(0.0))
    )
    
    final_orders.select(
        "order_id",
        "customer_name",
        "country",
        "amount_after_discount",
        "shipping_cost",
        "final_total",
        "delivery_days"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Step 5: Generate Business Analytics ---")
    
    # Revenue by membership tier
    revenue_by_tier = final_orders.groupBy("membership").agg(
        count("order_id").alias("order_count"),
        sum("total_amount").alias("gross_revenue"),
        sum("discount_amount").alias("total_discounts"),
        sum("final_total").alias("net_revenue"),
        avg("final_total").alias("avg_order_value")
    ).orderBy(desc("net_revenue"))
    
    print("\nRevenue by Membership Tier:")
    revenue_by_tier.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Top products
    top_products = order_details.groupBy("product_name", "category").agg(
        sum("quantity").alias("units_sold"),
        sum("item_total").alias("revenue")
    ).orderBy(desc("revenue"))
    
    print("\nTop Products:")
    top_products.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Geographic analysis
    geo_analysis = final_orders.groupBy("country", "zone").agg(
        count("order_id").alias("orders"),
        sum("final_total").alias("revenue"),
        avg("delivery_days").alias("avg_delivery_days")
    ).orderBy(desc("revenue"))
    
    print("\nGeographic Analysis:")
    geo_analysis.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Step 6: Identify Issues (Cache Lookup for Multiple Queries) ---")
    
    # Cache for multiple analytical queries
    final_orders.cache()
    final_orders.count()  # Materialize cache
    
    # Query 1: Cancelled orders
    cancelled_orders = final_orders.filter(col("status") == "cancelled")
    print(f"\nCancelled Orders: {cancelled_orders.count()}")
    cancelled_orders.select("order_id", "customer_name", "final_total").show()
    
    # Query 2: High-value orders
    high_value = final_orders.filter(col("final_total") > 300)
    print(f"\nHigh-Value Orders (>$300): {high_value.count()}")
    high_value.select("order_id", "customer_name", "final_total").show()
    
    # Query 3: Premium customers
    premium_orders = final_orders.filter(col("membership") == "Premium")
    print(f"\nPremium Customer Orders: {premium_orders.count()}")
    
    # Cleanup
    final_orders.unpersist()
    broadcast_discounts.unpersist()
    
    print("\n✓ E-commerce use case completed successfully!")


# ============================================================================
# OPTIMIZATION TIPS AND BEST PRACTICES
# ============================================================================
def optimization_tips():
    """
    Comprehensive optimization tips for lookup patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION TIPS & BEST PRACTICES")
    print("="*80)
    
    tips = """
    ╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                    LOOKUP PATTERN OPTIMIZATION GUIDE                      ║
    ╚═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    1. CHOOSING THE RIGHT PATTERN
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    📊 Lookup Table Size:
       • < 10 MB        → Use BROADCAST lookup
       • 10 MB - 1 GB   → Use CACHE + INDEX lookup
       • > 1 GB         → Use PARTITIONED or DIRECT lookup
    
    🔄 Access Frequency:
       • One-time       → DIRECT lookup
       • Few times      → BROADCAST lookup
       • Many times     → CACHE lookup
       • Continuous     → CACHE + BROADCAST
    
    💾 Memory
```python
 Available:
       • Limited        → DIRECT or INDEX lookup
       • Moderate       → CACHE or BROADCAST (selectively)
       • Abundant       → CACHE + BROADCAST aggressively
    
    ⚡ Performance Priority:
       • Speed critical → BROADCAST (if small) or HASH lookup
       • Memory critical→ DIRECT or INDEX lookup
       • Balanced       → CACHE lookup
    
    
    2. BROADCAST JOIN OPTIMIZATION
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    ✓ DO:
       • Use for dimension tables < 10 MB
       • Broadcast the smaller table explicitly
       • Filter dimension table before broadcasting
       • Select only needed columns before broadcasting
       • Monitor broadcast variable size
    
    ✗ DON'T:
       • Broadcast tables > 100 MB
       • Broadcast multiple large tables simultaneously
       • Forget to unpersist broadcast variables
       • Broadcast without filtering/projection
    
    Example:
    ```python
    # Good
    small_lookup = large_lookup.select("id", "name").filter(col("active") == True)
    result = fact_table.join(broadcast(small_lookup), "id")
    
    # Bad
    result = fact_table.join(broadcast(large_lookup), "id")  # Too large!
    ```
    
    
    3. CACHE OPTIMIZATION
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    ✓ DO:
       • Cache lookup tables used 3+ times
       • Use appropriate storage levels
       • Trigger caching with count() or first()
       • Unpersist when done
       • Monitor cache memory usage
    
    Storage Levels:
       • MEMORY_ONLY          → Fast, but may evict
       • MEMORY_AND_DISK      → Safer, slower fallback
       • MEMORY_ONLY_SER      → Compressed, slower access
       • DISK_ONLY            → Slowest, saves memory
    
    Example:
    ```python
    # Cache with specific storage level
    from pyspark import StorageLevel
    
    lookup_df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
    lookup_df.count()  # Materialize
    
    # Use multiple times
    result1 = fact_df.join(lookup_df, "key")
    result2 = fact_df.join(lookup_df, "key").filter(...)
    
    # Cleanup
    lookup_df.unpersist()
    ```
    
    
    4. PARTITIONING STRATEGIES
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    ✓ DO:
       • Partition both tables on join key
       • Use 2-3x number of cores for partition count
       • Coalesce after filtering to reduce partitions
       • Use salting for skewed data
    
    Partition Count Guidelines:
       • Small data (< 1 GB)    → 4-8 partitions
       • Medium data (1-10 GB)  → 8-32 partitions
       • Large data (> 10 GB)   → 32-200 partitions
    
    Example:
    ```python
    # Optimal partitioning
    num_partitions = spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism * 2
    
    fact_partitioned = fact_df.repartition(num_partitions, "join_key")
    dim_partitioned = dim_df.repartition(num_partitions, "join_key")
    
    result = fact_partitioned.join(dim_partitioned, "join_key")
    ```
    
    
    5. HANDLING DATA SKEW
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    Salting Technique:
    ```python
    # Add salt to skewed keys
    salt_range = 10
    
    fact_salted = fact_df.withColumn(
        "salt", (rand() * salt_range).cast("int")
    ).withColumn(
        "salted_key", concat(col("join_key"), lit("_"), col("salt"))
    )
    
    dim_exploded = dim_df.withColumn(
        "salt", explode(array([lit(i) for i in range(salt_range)]))
    ).withColumn(
        "salted_key", concat(col("join_key"), lit("_"), col("salt"))
    )
    
    result = fact_salted.join(dim_exploded, "salted_key")
    ```
    
    
    6. MEMORY MANAGEMENT
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    Monitor Memory:
    ```python
    # Check cache usage
    spark.catalog.clearCache()  # Clear all cached data
    
    # Monitor specific DataFrame
    df.cache()
    print(f"Cached: {df.is_cached}")
    print(f"Storage Level: {df.storageLevel}")
    
    # Selective caching
    df.select("important_cols").cache()  # Cache only needed columns
    ```
    
    
    7. QUERY OPTIMIZATION
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    ✓ DO:
       • Filter before joining
       • Select only needed columns
       • Use column pruning
       • Leverage predicate pushdown
       • Enable adaptive query execution
    
    Example:
    ```python
    # Good - Filter and project before join
    fact_filtered = fact_df.filter(col("date") >= "2024-01-01") \\
                           .select("id", "amount", "date")
    
    dim_filtered = dim_df.filter(col("active") == True) \\
                         .select("id", "name", "category")
    
    result = fact_filtered.join(broadcast(dim_filtered), "id")
    
    # Bad - Join then filter
    result = fact_df.join(dim_df, "id").filter(col("date") >= "2024-01-01")
    ```
    
    
    8. CONFIGURATION TUNING
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    Key Spark Configurations:
    ```python
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "10485760")  # 10MB
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin", "false")
    ```
    
    
    9. COMMON PITFALLS
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    ⚠️ Avoid:
       1. Broadcasting large tables (OOM errors)
       2. Not unpersisting cached data
       3. Over-partitioning small datasets
       4. Under-partitioning large datasets
       5. Joining on non-partitioned columns
       6. Collecting large lookup tables to driver
       7. Using UDFs when built-in functions work
       8. Not monitoring execution plans
    
    
    10. DEBUGGING AND MONITORING
    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    
    Useful Commands:
    ```python
    # View execution plan
    df.explain(mode="extended")  # or "simple", "cost", "formatted"
    
    # Check for broadcast
    df.explain()  # Look for BroadcastHashJoin

    ```

    ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    import time
    
    def benchmark_lookup(name, func):

        elapsed = time.time() - start
        print(f"{name}: {elapsed:.4f}s, {count} records")

    # Compare patterns

    print(f"Speedup: {direct_time/broadcast_time:.2f}x")

# ADVANCED PATTERN: INCREMENTAL LOOKUP
# ============================================================================
def incremental_lookup_pattern():
    """
    Advanced pattern for handling incremental/delta lookups
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ADVANCED PATTERN: INCREMENTAL LOOKUP")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Simulate historical and new data
    historical_customers = spark.createDataFrame([
        (101, "John Doe", "Gold", "2023-01-01"),
        (102, "Jane Smith", "Silver", "2023-02-01"),
        (103, "Bob Johnson", "Bronze", "2023-03-01"),
    ], ["customer_id", "customer_name", "tier", "effective_date"])
    
    new_customers = spark.createDataFrame([
        (104, "Alice Brown", "Gold", "2024-01-01"),
        (102, "Jane Smith", "Platinum", "2024-01-15"),  # Update
    ], ["customer_id", "customer_name", "tier", "effective_date"])
    
    transactions = spark.createDataFrame([
        (1, 101, "2024-01-10", 100.00),
        (2, 102, "2024-01-20", 200.00),
        (3, 104, "2024-01-05", 150.00),
    ], ["txn_id", "customer_id", "txn_date", "amount"])
    
    print("\n--- Method 1: SCD Type 2 Lookup (Slowly Changing Dimension) ---")
    
    # Combine historical and new data with versioning
    all_customers = historical_customers.unionByName(new_customers) \
        .withColumn("row_num", 
            row_number().over(
                Window.partitionBy("customer_id")
                      .orderBy(desc("effective_date"))
            )
        )
    
    # Get latest version
    current_customers = all_customers.filter(col("row_num") == 1).drop("row_num")
    
    print("Current Customer State:")
    current_customers.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Point-in-time lookup
    print("\n--- Point-in-Time Lookup ---")
    
    pit_lookup = transactions.join(
        all_customers,
        (transactions.customer_id == all_customers.customer_id) &
        (col("txn_date") >= col("effective_date")),
        "left"
    ).withColumn(
        "rank",
        row_number().over(
            Window.partitionBy("txn_id")
                  .orderBy(desc("effective_date"))
        )
    ).filter(col("rank") == 1).drop("rank", "row_num")
    
    print("Point-in-Time Lookup Result:")
    pit_lookup.select(
        "txn_id", "txn_date", "customer_name", "tier", "effective_date", "amount"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Method 2: Delta/Incremental Merge ---")
    
    # Merge logic
    merged_customers = historical_customers.alias("hist").join(
        new_customers.alias("new"),
        "customer_id",
        "full_outer"
    ).select(
        coalesce(col("new.customer_id"), col("hist.customer_id")).alias("customer_id"),
        coalesce(col("new.customer_name"), col("hist.customer_name")).alias("customer_name"),
        coalesce(col("new.tier"), col("hist.tier")).alias("tier"),
        coalesce(col("new.effective_date"), col("hist.effective_date")).alias("effective_date"),
        when(col("new.customer_id").isNotNull(), lit
("updated"))
        .when(col("hist.customer_id").isNull(), lit("new"))
        .otherwise(lit("unchanged")).alias("status")
    )
    
    print("Merged Customer Data:")
    merged_customers.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Use merged data for lookup
    enriched_txn = transactions.join(
        broadcast(merged_customers),
        "customer_id",
        "left"
    )
    
    print("\nEnriched Transactions with Merge Status:")
    enriched_txn.show(truncate=False)

# ADVANCED PATTERN: MULTI-KEY LOOKUP
# ============================================================================
def multi_key_lookup_pattern():
    """
    Advanced pattern for lookups with composite keys
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ADVANCED PATTERN: MULTI-KEY LOOKUP")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Create data with composite keys
    transactions = spark.createDataFrame([
        (1, "USA", "CA", "2024-01-01", 100.00),
        (2, "USA", "NY", "2024-01-02", 200.00),
        (3, "UK", "LDN", "2024-01-03", 150.00),
        (4, "USA", "CA", "2024-01-04", 120.00),
    ], ["txn_id", "country", "state", "txn_date", "amount"])
    
    # Tax rates by country and state
    tax_rates = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("USA", "CA", 0.0725),
        ("USA", "NY", 0.0400),
        ("UK", "LDN", 0.2000),
        ("USA", "TX", 0.0625),
    ], ["country", "state", "tax_rate"])
    
    print("\n--- Method 1: Direct Multi-Key Join ---")
    
    result1 = transactions.join(
        broadcast(tax_rates),
        ["country", "state"],
        "left"
    ).withColumn(
        "tax_amount",
        col("amount") * coalesce(col("tax_rate"), lit(0.0))
    ).withColumn(
        "total_with_tax",
        col("amount") + col("tax_amount")
    )
    
    print("Multi-Key Join Result:")
    result1.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Method 2: Composite Key String ---")
    
    # Create composite key
    transactions_comp = transactions.withColumn(
        "composite_key",
        concat_ws("|", col("country"), col("state"))
    )
    
    tax_rates_comp = tax_rates.withColumn(
        "composite_key",
        concat_ws("|", col("country"), col("state"))
    )
    
    result2 = transactions_comp.join(
        broadcast(tax_rates_comp.select("composite_key", "tax_rate")),
        "composite_key",
        "left"
    ).drop("composite_key")
    
    print("Composite Key Join Result:")
    result2.select("txn_id", "country", "state", "amount", "tax_rate").show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Method 3: Hash-Based Multi-Key Lookup ---")
    
    # Create hash map for multi-key lookup
    tax_dict = {
        (row['country'], row['state']): row['tax_rate']
        for row in tax_rates.collect()
    }
    broadcast_tax = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(tax_dict)
    
    @udf(DoubleType())
    def lookup_tax_rate(country, state):
        return broadcast_tax.value.get((country, state), 0.0)
    
    result3 = transactions.withColumn(
        "tax_rate",
        lookup_tax_rate(col("country"), col("state"))
    ).withColumn(
        "tax_amount",
        col("amount") * col("tax_rate")
    )
    
    print("Hash-Based Multi-Key Lookup Result:")
    result3.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Cleanup
    broadcast_tax.unpersist()

# ADVANCED PATTERN: RANGE LOOKUP
# ============================================================================
def range_lookup_pattern():
    """
    Advanced pattern for range-based lookups
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ADVANCED PATTERN: RANGE LOOKUP")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Transactions with amounts
    transactions = spark.createDataFrame([
        (1, 50.00),
        (2, 150.00),
        (3, 550.00),
        (4, 1500.00),
        (5, 5500.00),
    ], ["txn_id", "amount"])
    
    # Commission tiers (range-based)
    commission_tiers = spark.createDataFrame([
        (0.00, 100.00, 0.01),      # 1% for $0-$100
        (100.01, 500.00, 0.02),    # 2% for $100-$500
        (500.01, 1000.00, 0.03),   # 3% for $500-$1000
        (1000.01, 5000.00, 0.04),  # 4% for $1000-$5000
        (5000.01, 999999.99, 0.05),# 5% for $5000+
    ], ["min_amount", "max_amount", "commission_rate"])
    
    print("\n--- Method 1: Range Join ---")
    
    result1 = transactions.join(
        broadcast(commission_tiers),
        (col("amount") >= col("min_amount")) & 
        (col("amount") <= col("max_amount")),
        "left"
    ).withColumn(
        "commission",
        col("amount") * col("commission_rate")
    ).select(
        "txn_id",
        "amount",
        "min_amount",
        "max_amount",
        "commission_rate",
        "commission"
    )
    
    print("Range Join Result:")
    result1.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Method 2: Bucketing for Range Lookup ---")
    
    # Create buckets
    from pyspark.sql.functions import floor
    
    transactions_bucketed = transactions.withColumn(
        "bucket",
        floor(col("amount") / 1000)  # $1000 buckets
    )
    
    print("Bucketed Transactions:")
    transactions_bucketed.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Method 3: UDF-Based Range Lookup ---")
    
    # Create tier lookup function
    tier_list = [(row['min_amount'], row['max_amount'], row['commission_rate']) 
                 for row in commission_tiers.collect()]
    broadcast_tiers = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(tier_list)
    
    @udf(DoubleType())
    def find_commission_rate(amount):
        tiers = broadcast_tiers.value
        for min_amt, max_amt, rate in tiers:
            if min_amt <= amount <= max_amt:
                return rate
        return 0.0
    
    result3 = transactions.withColumn(
        "commission_rate",
        find_commission_rate(col("amount"))
    ).withColumn(
        "commission",
        col("amount") * col("commission_rate")
    )
    
    print("UDF-Based Range Lookup Result:")
    result3.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Cleanup
    broadcast_tiers.unpersist()


# ============================================================================
# ADVANCED PATTERN: CROSS-REFERENCE LOOKUP
# ============================================================================
def cross_reference_lookup_pattern():
    """
    Advanced pattern for cross-reference/mapping lookups
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ADVANCED PATTERN: CROSS-REFERENCE LOOKUP")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Source system data
    source_data = spark.createDataFrame([
        (1, "EXT001", "ProductA"),
        (2, "EXT002", "ProductB"),
        (3, "EXT003", "ProductC"),
    ], ["id", "external_id", "external_name"])
    
    # Cross-reference mapping
    xref_mapping = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("EXT001", "INT101", "System1"),
        ("EXT002", "INT102", "System1"),
        ("EXT003", "INT103", "System1"),
        ("EXT001", "ALT201", "System2"),  # Same external ID, different internal
    ], ["external_id", "internal_id", "system"])
    
    # Internal master data
    master_data = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("INT101", "Product Alpha", "Active"),
        ("INT102", "Product Beta", "Active"),
        ("INT103", "Product Gamma", "Inactive"),
        ("ALT201", "Product Alpha Alt", "Active"),
    ], ["internal_id", "master_name", "status"])
    
    print("\n--- Method 1: Multi-System Cross-Reference ---")
    
    # Join through cross-reference for specific system
    result1 = source_data.join(
        broadcast(xref_mapping.filter(col("system") == "System1")),
        "external_id",
        "left"
    ).join(
        broadcast(master_data),
        "internal_id",
        "left"
    ).select(
        "id",
        "external_id",
        "external_name",
        "internal_id",
        "master_name",
        "status"
    )
    
    print("Cross-Reference Lookup (System1):")
    result1.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Method 2: All Systems Cross-Reference ---")
    
    # Get all mappings
    result2 = source_data.join(
        broadcast(xref_mapping),
        "external_id",
        "left"
    ).join(
        broadcast(master_data),
        "internal_id",
        "left"
    ).select(
        "id",
        "external_id",
        "system",
        "internal_id",
        "master_name",
        "status"
    )
    
    print("Cross-Reference Lookup (All Systems):")
    result2.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Method 3: Preferred System with Fallback ---")
    
    # Priority-based lookup
    xref_with_priority = xref_mapping.withColumn(
        "priority",
        when(col("system") == "System1", 1)
        .when(col("system") == "System2", 2)
        .otherwise(99)
    )
    
    result3 = source_data.join(
        broadcast(xref_with_priority),
        "external_id",
        "left"
    ).withColumn(
        "rank",
        row_number().over(
            Window.partitionBy("id").orderBy("priority")
        )
    ).filter(col("rank") == 1).drop("rank", "priority") \
    .join(
        broadcast(master_data),
        "internal_id",
        "left"
    )
    
    print("Priority-Based Cross-Reference:")
    result3.select(
        "id", "external_id", "system", "internal_id", "master_name"
    ).show(truncate=False)

    │ Code:     df1.repartition("key").join(df2.repartition("key"), "key")      │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 3. CACHE LOOKUP PATTERN                                                   │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Usage:    In-memory caching for fast repeated access                      │
    │ Best For: Frequently accessed lookup tables                               │
    │ Code:     df2.cache(); df1.join(df2, "key")                               │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 4. BROADCAST LOOKUP PATTERN                                               │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Usage:    Distribute small table to all nodes                             │
    │ Best For: Small dimension tables (< 10MB)                                 │
    │ Code:     df1.join(broadcast(df2), "key")                                 │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 5. HASH LOOKUP PATTERN                                                    │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Usage:    Dictionary/map-based O(1) lookups                               │
    │ Best For: Custom logic, key-value pairs                                   │
    │ Code:     Use broadcast dict + UDF or map_from_entries                    │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    
    PATTERN SELECTION DECISION TREE:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    
    Is lookup table < 10MB?
    ├─ YES → Use BROADCAST LOOKUP
    └─ NO → Is it accessed multiple times?
           ├─ YES → Use CACHE LOOKUP
           └─ NO → Is data skewed or very large?
                  ├─ YES → Use INDEX LOOKUP (with partitioning)
                  └─
NO → Use DIRECT LOOKUP
    
    
    PERFORMANCE CHARACTERISTICS:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    
    Pattern          | Speed    | Memory    | Network   | Shuffle   | Best Use
    ─────────────────┼──────────┼───────────┼───────────┼───────────┼─────────
    Direct Lookup    | Moderate | Low       | High      | Yes       | One-time
    Index Lookup     | Good     | Moderate  | Moderate  | Reduced   | Large data
    Cache Lookup     | Fast     | High      | Low       | Yes       | Repeated
    Broadcast Lookup | Fastest  | Moderate  | Low       | No        | Small dim
    Hash Lookup      | Fastest  | High      | None      | No        | Custom
    
    
    ADVANCED PATTERNS COVERED:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    
    ✓ Multi-Level Lookup      - Chained lookups across multiple tables
    ✓ Conditional Lookup      - Different lookups based on conditions
    ✓ Fuzzy Lookup           - Approximate matching (soundex, levenshtein)
    ✓ Temporal Lookup        - Time-based/historical lookups
    ✓ Hierarchical Lookup    - Parent-child relationships
    ✓ Incremental Lookup     - Delta/SCD handling
    ✓ Multi-Key Lookup       - Composite key lookups
    ✓ Range Lookup           - Value range-based lookups
    ✓ Cross-Reference Lookup - System mapping lookups
    
    
    KEY TAKEAWAYS:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    
    1. Always broadcast small dimension tables (< 10MB)
    2. Cache frequently accessed lookup tables
    3. Partition large datasets on join keys
    4. Filter and project before joining
    5. Monitor memory usage and unpersist when done
    6. Use appropriate join types (left, inner, etc.)
    7. Handle null keys and missing lookups gracefully
    8. Enable adaptive query execution
    9. Test with production-scale data
    10. Monitor execution plans regularly
    
    
    COMMON ISSUES AND SOLUTIONS:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    
    Issue: Out of Memory (OOM)
    Solution: Reduce broadcast threshold, use partitioning, unpersist caches
    
    Issue: Slow joins
    Solution: Use broadcast for small tables, partition on join keys
    
    Issue: Data skew
    Solution: Use salting technique, enable skew join optimization
    
    Issue: Missing lookups
    Solution: Use left join, provide default values with coalesce
    
    Issue: Duplicate keys in lookup
    Solution: Deduplicate using window functions before join
    
    
    SPARK CONFIGURATION RECOMMENDATIONS:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# 1. ROW FORMAT PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Purpose: Format each row as a single structured entity
# Use Case: API responses, JSON exports, row-level transformations

print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("1. ROW FORMAT PATTERN")
print("=" * 80)

class RowFormatPattern:
    """
    Formats query results where each row is treated as a complete entity.
    Useful for creating JSON documents, API responses, or row-based exports.
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_as_struct(df):
        """
        Format entire row as a nested struct
        """
        print("\n--- Format as Struct ---")
        
        # Create a struct containing all employee information
        result = df.select(
            struct(
                col("emp_id"),
                col("first_name"),
                col("last_name"),
                col("department"),
                col("salary"),
                col("location"),
                col("email")
            ).alias("employee_record")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        result.printSchema()
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_as_json(df):
        """
        Format each row as a JSON string
        """
        print("\n--- Format as JSON ---")
        
        # Convert entire row to JSON
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            to_json(
                struct(
                    col("first_name"),
                    col("last_name"),
                    col("department"),
                    col("salary"),
                    col("location"),
                    col("email")
                )
            ).alias("employee_json")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_as_key_value(df):
        """
        Format row as key-value pairs
        """
        print("\n--- Format as Key-Value Pairs ---")
        
        # Create a map of column names to values
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            map_from_arrays(
                array(
                    lit("first_name"), lit("last_name"), lit("department"),
                    lit("salary"), lit("location"), lit("email")
                ),
                array(
                    col("first_name"), col("last_name"), col("department"),
                    col("salary").cast("string"), col("location"), col("email")
                )
            ).alias("employee_map")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_with_metadata(df):
        """
        Format row with additional metadata
        """
        print("\n--- Format with Metadata ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import current_timestamp, monotonically_increasing_id
        
        result = df.select(
            struct(
                monotonically_increasing_id().alias("record_id"),
                current_timestamp().alias("created_at"),
                struct(
                    col("emp_id"),
                    col("first_name"),
                    col("last_name"),
                    col("department"),
                    col("salary"),
                    col("location"),
                    col("email")
                ).alias("data")
            ).alias("employee_with_metadata")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result

# Execute Row Format Pattern examples

row_formatter.format_as_key_value(employees_df)

print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("2. COLUMN FORMAT PATTERN")
print("=" * 80)

class ColumnFormatPattern:
    """
    Applies formatting transformations to individual columns.
    Useful for display formatting, data masking, and column-level transformations.
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_currency(df):
        """
        Format salary column as currency
        """
        print("\n--- Format Currency ---")
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("full_name"),
            col("department"),
            format_string("$%,.2f", col("salary")).alias("formatted_salary"),
            col("location")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_names(df):
        """
        Format name columns with proper capitalization
        """
        print("\n--- Format Names ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import upper, lower, initcap
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            upper(col("first_name")).alias("first_name_upper"),
            lower(col("last_name")).alias("last_name_lower"),
            initcap(concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name"))).alias("full_name_proper"),
            col("department")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_masked_data(df):
        """
        Format sensitive columns with masking
        """
        print("\n--- Format Masked Data ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import regexp_replace, substring
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            col("first_name"),
            col("last_name"),
            # Mask email - show only first 3 chars and domain
            concat(
                substring(col("email"), 1, 3),
                lit("***@"),
                expr("split(email, '@')[1]")
            ).alias("masked_email"),
            # Mask salary - show only range
            when(col("salary") < 70000, "< $70K")
            .when(col("salary") < 80000, "$70K - $80K")
            .otherwise("> $80K").alias("salary_range")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_conditional(df):
        """
        Apply conditional formatting to columns
        """
        print("\n--- Format Conditional ---")
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("name"),
            col("department"),
            col("salary"),
            # Add performance indicator based on salary
            when(col("salary") >= 80000, "⭐ High Performer")
            .when(col("salary") >= 70000, "✓ Good Performer")
            .otherwise("→ Standard").alias("performance_indicator"),
            # Format location with emoji
            concat(lit("📍 "), col("location")).alias("formatted_location")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result

# Execute Column Format Pattern examples

column_formatter.format_currency(employees_df)
column_formatter.format_names(employees_df)
column_formatter.format_masked_data(employees_df)
column_formatter.format_conditional(employees_df)

class NestedFormatPattern:
    """
    Creates nested and hierarchical data structures.
    Useful for complex JSON outputs, hierarchical data, and grouped aggregations.
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_grouped_nested(df):
        """
        Group data and create nested structures
        """
        print("\n--- Format Grouped Nested ---")
        
        # Group employees by department with nested employee details
        result = df.groupBy("department").agg(
            collect_list(
                struct(
                    col("emp_id"),
                    col("first_name"),
                    col("last_name"),
                    col("salary"),
                    col("location"),
                    col("email")
                )
            ).alias("employees")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        result.printSchema()
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_multi_level_nested(df):
        """
        Create multi-level nested structure
        """
        print("\n--- Format Multi-Level Nested ---")
        
        result = df.groupBy("department", "location").agg(
            struct(
                collect_list(
                    struct(
                        col("emp_id"),
                        struct(
                            col("first_name"),
                            col("last_name")
                        ).alias("name"),
                        col("salary"),
                        col("email")
                    )
                ).alias("employees"),
                expr("avg(salary)").alias("avg_salary"),
                expr("count(*)").alias("employee_count")
            ).alias("location_details")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        result.printSchema()
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_nested_with_arrays(df):
        """
        Create nested structures with arrays
        """
        print("\n--- Format Nested with Arrays ---")
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            struct(
                struct(
                    col("first_name"),
                    col("last_name")
                ).alias("name"),
                struct(
                    col("department"),
                    col("location")
                ).alias("work_info"),
                struct(
                    col("salary"),
                    (col("salary") * 0.15).alias("bonus"),
                    (col("salary") * 1.15).alias("total_compensation")
                ).alias("compensation"),
                array(col("email")).alias("contact_methods")
            ).alias("employee_profile")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        result.printSchema()
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_hierarchical_json(df):
        """
        Create hierarchical JSON structure
        """
        print("\n--- Format Hierarchical JSON ---")
        
        # Create a complex nested structure and convert to JSON
        nested_df = df.groupBy("department").agg(
            struct(
                col("department").alias("department_name"),
                collect_list(
                    struct(
                        col("emp_id"),
                        struct(
                            col("first_name"),
                            col("last_name"),
                            col("email")
                        ).alias("personal_info"),
                        struct(
                            col("salary"),
                            col("location")
                        ).alias("employment_details")
                    )
                ).alias("team_members"),
                expr("count(*)").alias("team_size"),
                expr("avg(salary)").alias("avg_team_salary")
            ).alias("department_info")
        )
        
        result = nested_df.select(
            col("department"),
            to_json(col("department_info")).alias("department_json")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result

# Execute Nested Format Pattern examples

            col("contact.value").alias("contact_value")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def flatten_json_to_columns(df):
        """
        Flatten JSON strings into columns
        """
        print("\n--- Flatten JSON to Columns ---")
        
        # Create JSON column
        json_df = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            to_json(
                struct(
                    col("first_name"),
                    col("last_name"),
                    col("department"),
                    col("salary")
                )
            ).alias("employee_json")
        )
        
        # Define schema for JSON
        json_schema = StructType([
            StructField("first_name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("last_name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("department", StringType(), True),
            StructField("salary", IntegerType(), True)
        ])
        
        # Parse and flatten JSON
        result = json_df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            from_json(col("employee_json"), json_schema).alias("parsed")
        ).select(
            col("emp_id"),
            col("parsed.first_name").alias("first_name"),
            col("parsed.last_name").alias("last_name"),
            col("parsed.department").alias("department"),
            col("parsed.salary").alias("salary")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def flatten_complex_hierarchy(df):
        """
        Flatten complex multi-level hierarchy
        """
        print("\n--- Flatten Complex Hierarchy ---")
        
        # Create complex nested structure
        complex_df = df.groupBy("department").agg(
            collect_list(
                struct(
                    col("emp_id"),
                    col("first_name"),
                    col("last_name"),
                    col("salary")
                )
            ).alias("employees")
        )
        
        # Flatten by exploding and selecting
        result = complex_df.select(
            col("department"),
            explode(col("employees")).alias("employee")
        ).select(
            col("department"),
            col("employee.emp_id").alias("emp_id"),
            col("employee.first_name").alias("first_name"),
            col("employee.last_name").alias("last_name"),
            col("employee.salary").alias("salary")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result

# Execute Flat Format Pattern examples

flat_formatter.flatten_nested_struct(employees_df)
flat_formatter.flatten_array_to_columns(employees_df)
flat_formatter.flatten_explode_arrays(employees_df)
flat_formatter.flatten_json_to_columns(employees_df)
flat_formatter.flatten_complex_hierarchy(employees_df)

class CustomFormatPattern:
    """
    Implements custom formatting logic based on business requirements.
    Allows for complex transformations, custom templates, and business rules.
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_custom_template(df):
        """
        Apply custom string template formatting
        """
        print("\n--- Custom Template Format ---")
        
        # Create custom formatted output using template
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            format_string(
                "Employee: %s %s | Dept: %s | Salary: $%,.2f | Location: %s",
                col("first_name"),
                col("last_name"),
                col("department"),
                col("salary"),
                col("location")
            ).alias("employee_summary")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_business_rules(df):
        """
        Apply complex business rules for formatting
        """
        print("\n--- Business Rules Format ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import round
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("full_name"),
            col("department"),
            col("salary"),
            # Calculate bonus based on department and salary
            when(col("department") == "Engineering", col("salary") * 0.20)
            .when(col("department") == "Sales", col("salary") * 0.25)
            .when(col("department") == "Marketing", col("salary") * 0.15)
            .otherwise(col("salary") * 0.10).alias("bonus"),
            # Performance rating
            when((col("department") == "Engineering") & (col("salary") >= 80000), "A+")
            .when((col("department") == "Engineering") & (col("salary") >= 75000), "A")
            .when(col("salary") >= 70000, "B+")
            .otherwise("B").alias("performance_rating"),
            # Custom status
            when(col("location") == "New York", "HQ Employee")
            .otherwise("Regional Employee").alias("employee_status")
        ).withColumn(
            "total_compensation",
            round(col("salary") + col("bonus"), 2)
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_report_style(df):
        """
        Format data in a report-friendly style
        """
        print("\n--- Report Style Format ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import lpad, rpad
        
        result = df.select(
            # Fixed-width formatting for report
            lpad(col("emp_id").cast("string"), 5, "0").alias("ID"),
            rpad(
                concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")), 
                25, 
                " "
            ).alias("Name"),
            rpad(col("department"), 15, " ").alias("Department"),
            lpad(format_string("$%,.2f", col("salary")), 12, " ").alias("Salary"),
            rpad(col("location"), 15, " ").alias("Location")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_custom_aggregation(df):
        """
        Custom aggregation with formatted output
        """
        print("\n--- Custom Aggregation Format ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import count, avg, min, max, stddev
        
        result = df.groupBy("department").agg(
            count("*").alias("employee_count"),
            round(avg("salary"), 2).alias("avg_salary"),
            min("salary").alias("min_salary"),
            max("salary").alias("max_salary"),
            round(stddev("salary"), 2).alias("salary_stddev")
        ).select(
            col("department"),
            col("employee_count"),
            # Format as custom summary string
            format_string(
                "Team Size: %d | Avg: $%,.2f | Range: $%,.2f - $%,.2f | StdDev: $%,.2f",
                col("employee_count"),
                col("avg_salary"),
                col("min_salary"),
                col("max_salary"),
                col("salary_stddev")
            ).alias("department_summary")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_pivot_style(df):
        """
        Create pivot-style custom format
        """
        print("\n--- Pivot Style Format ---")
        
        # Create a pivot-like structure with custom formatting
        result = df.groupBy("location").pivot("department").agg(
            concat_ws(
                ", ",
                collect_list(
                    concat(
                        col("first_name"),
                        lit(" ("),
                        format_string("$%,.0f", col("salary")),
                        lit(")")
                    )
                )
            )
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_custom_udf(df):
        """
        Use UDF for complex custom formatting
        """
        print("\n--- Custom UDF Format ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
        from pyspark.sql.types import StringType
        
        # Define custom formatting UDF
        def custom_employee_badge(first_name, last_name, emp_id, department):
            """
            Generate a custom employee badge format
            """
            badge = f"""
┌────────────────────────────┐
│ EMPLOYEE BADGE             │
├────────────────────────────┤
│ ID: {str(emp_id).zfill(5)}                  │
│ Name: {first_name} {last_name:<15} │
│ Dept: {department:<20} │
└────────────────────────────┘
            """.strip()
            return badge
        
        # Register UDF
        badge_udf = udf(custom_employee_badge, StringType())
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            badge_udf(
                col("first_name"),
                col("last_name"),
                col("emp_id"),
                col("department")
            ).alias("employee_badge")
        )
        
        result.show(5, truncate=False)
        return result
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_conditional_complex(df):
        """
        Complex conditional formatting with multiple rules
        """
        print("\n--- Complex Conditional Format ---")
        
        result = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("name"),
            col("department"),
            col("salary"),
            col("location"),
            # Multi-condition formatting
            when(
                (col("department") == "Engineering") & 
                (col("location") == "New York") & 
                (col("salary") >= 80000),
                struct(
                    lit("Senior Engineer - HQ").alias("title"),
                    lit("Level 3").alias("level"),
                    lit("🌟🌟🌟").alias("rating"),
                    (col("salary") * 0.25).alias("bonus_amount")
                )
            ).when(
                (col("department") == "Engineering") & 
                (col("salary") >= 75000),
                struct(
                    lit("Engineer").alias("title"),
                    lit("Level 2").alias("level"),
                    lit("🌟🌟").alias("rating"),
                    (col("salary") * 0.20).alias("bonus_amount")
                )
            ).when(
                col("department") == "Sales",
                struct(
                    lit("Sales Representative").alias("title"),
                    lit("Level 2").alias("level"),
                    lit("🌟🌟").alias("rating"),
                    (col("salary") * 0.30).alias("bonus_amount")
                )
            ).otherwise(
                struct(
                    col("department").alias("title"),
                    lit("Level 1").alias("level"),
                    lit("🌟").alias("rating"),
                    (col("salary") * 0.10).alias("bonus_amount")
                )
            ).alias("employee_classification")
        ).select(
            col("emp_id"),
            col("name"),
            col("department"),
            col("salary"),
            col("employee_classification.title").alias("job_title"),
            col("employee_classification.level").alias("job_level"),
            col("employee_classification.rating").alias("performance_rating"),
            round(col("employee_classification.bonus_amount"), 2).alias("bonus")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result

# Execute Custom Format Pattern examples
custom_formatter = CustomFormatPattern()
custom_formatter.format_custom_template(employees_df)
custom_formatter.format_business_rules(employees_df)
custom_formatter.format_report_style(employees_df)
custom_formatter.format_custom_aggregation(employees_df)
custom_formatter.format_pivot_style(employees_df)
custom_formatter.format_custom_udf(employees_df)
custom_formatter.format_conditional_complex(employees_df)

class ComprehensiveFormattingExample:
    """
    Demonstrates combining multiple formatting patterns for real-world scenarios
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def generate_executive_report(df):
        """
        Generate an executive report combining multiple formatting patterns
        """
        print("\n--- Executive Report (Multi-Pattern) ---")
        
        # Step 1: Apply column formatting
        formatted_df = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("full_name"),
            col("department"),
            col("salary"),
            col("location")
        )
        
        # Step 2: Create nested structure by department
        nested_report = formatted_df.groupBy("department").agg(
            struct(
                count("*").alias("headcount"),
                round(avg("salary"), 2).alias("avg_salary"),
                min("salary").alias("min_salary"),
                max("salary").alias("max_salary"),
                collect_list(
                    struct(
                        col("emp_id"),
                        col("full_name"),
                        col("salary"),
                        col("location")
                    )
                ).alias("employees")
            ).alias("department_stats")
        )
        
        # Step 3: Apply custom formatting
        final_report = nested_report.select(
            col("department"),
            col("department_stats.headcount").alias("total_employees"),
            format_string("$%,.2f", col("department_stats.avg_salary")).alias("average_salary"),
            format_string(
                "$%,.
```python
                "$%,.2f - $%,.2f",
                col("department_stats.min_salary"),
                col("department_stats.max_salary")
            ).alias("salary_range"),
            col("department_stats.employees").alias("employee_details")
        )
        
        final_report.show(truncate=False)
        
        # Step 4: Flatten for CSV export
        print("\n--- Flattened for Export ---")
        flattened = final_report.select(
            col("department"),
            explode(col("employee_details")).alias("employee")
        ).select(
            col("department"),
            col("employee.emp_id").alias("emp_id"),
            col("employee.full_name").alias("name"),
            format_string("$%,.2f", col("employee.salary")).alias("salary"),
            col("employee.location").alias("location")
        )
        
        flattened.show(truncate=False)
        return final_report
    
    @staticmethod
    def generate_api_response(df):
        """
        Generate API-ready JSON response with multiple formatting patterns
        """
        print("\n--- API Response Format ---")
        
        # Create hierarchical structure
        api_response = df.groupBy("department").agg(
            struct(
                col("department").alias("department_name"),
                count("*").alias("employee_count"),
                struct(
                    round(avg("salary"), 2).alias("average"),
                    min("salary").alias("minimum"),
                    max("salary").alias("maximum")
                ).alias("salary_stats"),
                collect_list(
                    struct(
                        col("emp_id").alias("id"),
                        struct(
                            col("first_name"),
                            col("last_name"),
                            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("full_name")
                        ).alias("name"),
                        struct(
                            col("email"),
                            col("location")
                        ).alias("contact"),
                        struct(
                            col("salary"),
                            (col("salary") * 0.15).alias("estimated_bonus")
                        ).alias("compensation")
                    )
                ).alias("employees")
            ).alias("data")
        ).select(
            to_json(col("data")).alias("json_response")
        )
        
        api_response.show(truncate=False)
        return api_response
    
    @staticmethod
    def generate_dashboard_metrics(df):
        """
        Generate dashboard-ready metrics with custom formatting
        """
        print("\n--- Dashboard Metrics ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.window import Window
        from pyspark.sql.functions import rank, percent_rank, row_number
        
        # Calculate rankings
        salary_window = Window.orderBy(col("salary").desc())
        dept_window = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
        
        dashboard_data = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("name"),
            col("department"),
            col("salary"),
            col("location"),
            rank().over(salary_window).alias("company_rank"),
            rank().over(dept_window).alias("dept_rank"),
            round(percent_rank().over(salary_window) * 100, 2).alias("percentile")
        )
        
        # Format for dashboard
        result = dashboard_data.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            col("name"),
            col("department"),
            format_string("$%,.2f", col("salary")).alias("salary"),
            col("location"),
            format_string("#%d Overall", col("company_rank")).alias("company_ranking"),
            format_string("#%d in Dept", col("dept_rank")).alias("department_ranking"),
            format_string("Top %,.1f%%", lit(100) - col("percentile")).alias("performance_percentile"),
            # Add visual indicators
            when(col("company_rank") <= 2, "🥇 Top Performer")
            .when(col("company_rank") <= 5, "⭐ High Performer")
            .otherwise("✓ Good Standing").alias("status_badge")
        )
        
        result.show(truncate=False)
        return result

# Execute Comprehensive Examples
comprehensive = ComprehensiveFormattingExample()
comprehensive.generate_executive_report(employees_df)
comprehensive.generate_api_response(employees_df)
comprehensive.generate_dashboard_metrics(employees_df)

class FormattingUtilities:
    """
    Reusable utility functions for common formatting operations
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_percentage(value_col, total_col, decimal_places=2):
        """
        Format a value as percentage of total
        """
        from pyspark.sql.functions import round
        return concat(
            round((col(value_col) / col(total_col)) * 100, decimal_places).cast("string"),
            lit("%")
        )
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_phone_number(phone_col):
        """
        Format phone number with standard pattern
        """
        return format_string("(%s) %s-%s",
            expr(f"substring({phone_col}, 1, 3)"),
            expr(f"substring({phone_col}, 4, 3)"),
            expr(f"substring({phone_col}, 7, 4)")
        )
    
    @staticmethod
    def create_audit_columns(df):
        """
        Add standard audit columns to any dataframe
        """
        from pyspark.sql.functions import current_timestamp, current_date, lit
        
        return df.withColumn("created_at", current_timestamp()) \
                 .withColumn("created_date", current_date()) \
                 .withColumn("created_by", lit("system")) \
                 .withColumn("record_version", lit(1))
    
    @staticmethod
    def safe_divide(numerator_col, denominator_col, default_value=0):
        """
        Safely divide two columns, handling division by zero
        """
        return when(col(denominator_col) != 0, 
                   col(numerator_col) / col(denominator_col)
        ).otherwise(default_value)
    
    @staticmethod
    def format_null_values(df, replacement="N/A"):
        """
        Replace null values with a standard replacement across all string columns
        """
        from pyspark.sql.functions import coalesce
        
        for column in df.columns:
            if dict(df.dtypes)[column] == 'string':
                df = df.withColumn(column, coalesce(col(column), lit(replacement)))
        return df
    
    @staticmethod
    def standardize_column_names(df):
        """
        Standardize column names (lowercase, replace spaces with underscores)
        """
        for column in df.columns:
            new_name = column.lower().replace(" ", "_").replace("-", "_")
            df = df.withColumnRenamed(column, new_name)
        return df

# Demonstrate utility functions
print("\n--- Utility Functions Demo ---")

# Add audit columns

audited_df.select("emp_id", "first_name", "created_at", "created_date", "created_by").show(3)

print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION TIPS")
print("=" * 80)

class PerformanceOptimization:
    """
    Best practices for performance optimization in formatting operations
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def demonstrate_caching():
        """
        Demonstrate when to cache formatted results
        """
        print("\n--- Caching Strategy ---")
        
        # For expensive formatting operations that will be reused
        formatted_df = employees_df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("full_name"),
            col("department"),
            col("salary")
        )
        
        # Cache if this will be used multiple times
        formatted_df.cache()
        
        print(f"Cached dataframe with {formatted_df.count()} rows")
        
        # Use the cached dataframe multiple times
        formatted_df.groupBy("department").count().show()
        formatted_df.filter(col("salary") > 70000).show()
        
        # Don't forget to unpersist when done
        formatted_df.unpersist()
        print("Cache cleared")
    
    @staticmethod
    def demonstrate_partitioning():
        """
        Demonstrate optimal partitioning for formatting operations
        """
        print("\n--- Partitioning Strategy ---")
        
        # Repartition before expensive operations
        optimized_df = employees_df.repartition(4, "department")
        
        result = optimized_df.groupBy("department").agg(
            collect_list(
                struct(
                    col("emp_id"),
                    col("first_name"),
                    col("last_name"),
                    col("salary")
                )
            ).alias("employees")
        )
        
        print(f"Number of partitions: {result.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
        result.show()
    
    @staticmethod
    def demonstrate_broadcast():
        """
        Demonstrate broadcast joins for formatting with lookup tables
        """
        print("\n--- Broadcast Join Strategy ---")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
        
        # Create a small lookup table
        dept_info = spark.createDataFrame([
            ("Engineering", "ENG", "Technology"),
            ("Marketing", "MKT", "Business"),
            ("Sales", "SLS", "Business")
        ], ["department", "dept_code", "division"])
        
        # Use broadcast for small lookup table
        result = employees_df.join(
            broadcast(dept_info),
            "department",
            "left"
        ).select(
            col("emp_id"),
            concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("name"),
            col("department"),
            col("dept_code"),
            col("division"),
            col("salary")
        )
        
        result.show()
    
    @staticmethod
    def demonstrate_projection_pushdown():
        """
        Demonstrate selecting only needed columns early
        """
        print("\n--- Projection Pushdown ---")
        
        # BAD: Select all columns then filter
        # result = employees_df.filter(col("salary") > 70000).select("emp_id", "first_name")
        
        # GOOD: Select needed columns first
        result = employees_df.select("emp_id", "first_name", "salary") \
                            .filter(col("salary") > 70000)
        
        result.show()
        print("Selected only necessary columns before filtering")

# Execute Performance Optimization examples
perf_optimizer = PerformanceOptimization()
perf_optimizer.demonstrate_caching()
perf_optimizer.demonstrate_partitioning()
perf_optimizer.demonstrate_broadcast()
perf_optimizer.demonstrate_projection_pushdown()

    @staticmethod
    def export_to_parquet(df, output_path="/tmp/employees_parquet"):
        """
        Export formatted data as Parquet with nested structures
        """
        print("\n--- Export to Parquet ---")
        
        # Format with nested structures (efficient for Parquet)
        parquet_df = df.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            struct(
                col("first_name"),
                col("last_name"),
                concat(col("first_name"), lit(" "), col("last_name")).alias("full_name")
            ).alias("name"),
            struct(
                col("department"),
                col("location")
            ).alias("work_info"),
            struct(
                col("salary"),
                col("email")
            ).alias("details")
        )
        
        # Write to Parquet (commented out to avoid file system operations)
        # parquet_df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(output_path)
        
        print(f"Parquet export prepared (would write to {output_path})")
        parquet_df.printSchema()
        parquet_df.show(3, truncate=False)
