        (2, '[{"name":"Charlie","score":92}]')
    ]
    
    df_json_array = spark.createDataFrame(json_array_data, ["id", "json_data"])
    
    json_element_schema = ArrayType(StructType([
        StructField("name", StringType(), True),
        StructField("score", IntegerType(), True)
    ]))
    
    df_parsed_array = df_json_array.select(
        col("id"),
        from_json(col("json_data"), json_element_schema).alias("scores")
    )
    
    df_parsed_array.show(truncate=False)
    df_parsed_array.printSchema()
    
    # Explode the array
    print("\nExploded JSON Array:")
    df_parsed_array.select(
        col("id"),
        explode(col("scores")).alias("score_data")
    ).select(
        "id",
        "score_data.name",
        "score_data.score"
    ).show()
    
    # Pattern 5: Convert entire row to JSON
    print("\nPattern 5: Convert Entire Row to JSON:")
    df_row_json = df_serial.select(
        to_json(struct("*")).alias("row_json")
    )
    
    df_row_json.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 6: Partial serialization
    print("\nPattern 6: Partial Serialization:")
    df_partial = df_serial.select(
        col("id"),
        to_json(struct(
            col("user.name").alias("name"),
            col("user.age").alias("age")
        )).alias("user_summary_json"),
        col("metadata")
    )
    
    df_partial.show(truncate=False)
    
    return df_serial


# ============================================================================
# TYPE CONVERSION AND CASTING PATTERNS
# ============================================================================

def type_conversion_patterns():
    """
    Demonstrates type conversion and casting patterns between different data types.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("TYPE CONVERSION AND CASTING PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import (
        col, cast, array, create_map, struct, 
        split, concat_ws, map_from_arrays
    )
    
    # Sample data for conversions
    conversion_schema = StructType([
        StructField("id", IntegerType(), False),
        StructField("value_string", StringType(), True),
        StructField("value_int", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("value_double", DoubleType(), True),
        StructField("csv_values", StringType(), True),
        StructField("key_value_string", StringType(), True)
    ])
    
    conversion_data = [
        (1, "123", 456, 78.9, "a,b,c,d", "key1:value1,key2:value2"),
        (2, "789", 101, 11.2, "x,y,z", "name:Alice,age:30"),
        (3, "456", 202, 33.4, "p,q", "city:NYC,country:USA")
    ]
    
    df_conversion = spark.createDataFrame(conversion_data, conversion_schema)
    
    print("\nOriginal Data:")
    df_conversion.show(truncate=False)
    df_conversion.printSchema()
    
    # Pattern 1: Primitive type conversions
    print("\nPattern 1: Primitive Type Conversions:")
    df_primitive_cast = df_conversion.select(
        col("id"),
        # String to numeric
        col("value_string").cast(IntegerType()).alias("string_to_int"),
        col("value_string").cast(DoubleType()).alias("string_to_double"),
        # Numeric to string
        col("value_int").cast(StringType()).alias("int_to_string"),
        col("value_double").cast(StringType()).alias("double_to_string"),
        # Numeric conversions
        col("value_int").cast(DoubleType()).alias("int_to_double"),
        col("value_double").cast(IntegerType()).alias("double_to_int")
    )
    
    df_primitive_cast.show(truncate=False)
    df_primitive_cast.printSchema()
    
    # Pattern 2: String to Array conversion
    print("\nPattern 2: String to Array Conversion:")
    df_string_to_array = df_conversion.select(
        col("id"),
        col("csv_values"),
        split(col("csv_values"), ",").alias("array_values")
    )
    
    df_string_to_array.show(truncate=False)
    df_string_to_array.printSchema()
    
    # Pattern 3: Array to String conversion
    print("\nPattern 3: Array to String Conversion:")
    df_array_to_string = df_string_to_array.select(
        col("id"),
        col("array_values"),
        concat_ws("|", col("array_values")).alias("pipe_separated"),
        concat_ws(", ", col("array_values")).alias("comma_separated")
    )
    
    df_array_to_string.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 4: String to Map conversion
    print("\nPattern 4: String to Map Conversion:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import expr
    
    df_string_to_map = df_conversion.select(
        col("id"),
        col("key_value_string"),
        # Split and convert to map
        expr("str_to_map(key_value_string, ',', ':')").alias("map_values")
    )
    
    df_string_to_map.show(truncate=False)
    df_string_to_map.printSchema()
    
    # Pattern 5: Map to Array conversion
    print("\nPattern 5: Map to Array Conversion:")
    df_map_to_array = df_string_to_map.select(
        col("id"),
        col("map_values"),
        map_keys(col("map_values")).alias("keys_array"),
        map_values(col("map_values")).alias("values_array"),
        map_entries(col("map_values")).alias("entries_array")
    )
    
    df_map_to_array.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 6: Columns to Struct conversion
    print("\nPattern 6: Columns to Struct Conversion:")
    df_cols_to_struct = df_conversion.select(
        col("id"),
        struct(
            col("value_string").alias("str_val"),
            col("value_int").alias("int_val"),
            col("value_double").alias("dbl_val")
        ).alias("value_struct")
    )
    
    df_cols_to_struct.show(truncate=False)
    df_cols_to_struct.printSchema()
    
    # Pattern 7: Struct to Columns conversion (flattening)
    print("\nPattern 7: Struct to Columns Conversion:")
    df_struct_to_cols = df_cols_to_struct.select(
        col("id"),
        col("value_struct.str_val").alias("string_value"),
        col("value_struct.int_val").alias("integer_value"),
        col("value_struct.dbl_val").alias("double_value")
    )
    
    df_struct_to_cols.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 8: Arrays to Map conversion
    print("\nPattern 8: Arrays to Map Conversion:")
    df_arrays = df_conversion.select(
        col("id"),
        split(col("csv_values"), ",").alias("keys"),
        array(col("value_int"), col("value_int") + 1, col("value_int") + 2).alias("values")
    )
    
    df_arrays_to_map = df_arrays.select(
        col("id"),
        col("keys"),
        col("values"),
        map_from_arrays(col("keys"), col("values").cast(ArrayType(StringType()))).alias("created_map")
    )
    
    df_arrays_to_map.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 9: Complex nested conversions
    print("\nPattern 9: Complex Nested Conversions:")
    df_complex_conversion = df_conversion.select(
        col("id"),
        struct(
            col("value_string").alias("original"),
            col("value_string").cast(IntegerType()).alias("as_int"),
            struct(
                split(col("csv_values"), ",").alias("array"),
                size(split(col("csv_values"), ",")).alias("count")
            ).alias("array_info")
        ).alias("conversion_details")
    )
    
    df_complex_conversion.show(truncate=False)
    df_complex_conversion.printSchema()
    
    # Pattern 10: Safe type conversions with error handling
    print("\nPattern 10: Safe Type Conversions:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import when, col
    
    # Add some invalid data
    invalid_data = [
        (4, "not_a_number", 999, 88.8, "a,b", "k:v"),
        (5, "12.34", 111, 22.2, "x", "m:n")
    ]
    
    df_with_invalid = spark.createDataFrame(
        conversion_data + invalid_data, 
        conversion_schema
    )
    
    df_safe_conversion = df_with_invalid.select(
        col("id"),
        col("value_string"),
        # Safe conversion with fallback
        when(col("value_string").rlike("^[0-9]+$"), 
             col("value_string").cast(IntegerType()))
        .otherwise(lit(-1)).alias("safe_int_conversion"),
        # Validation before conversion
        when(col("value_string").rlike("^[0-9]+$"), lit("Valid"))
        .otherwise(lit("Invalid")).alias("validation_status")
    )
    
    df_safe_conversion.show(truncate=False)
    
    return df_conversion


# ============================================================================
# WINDOW FUNCTIONS WITH COMPLEX TYPES
# ============================================================================

def window_functions_with_complex_types():
    """
    Demonstrates window functions with complex data types.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("WINDOW FUNCTIONS WITH COMPLEX TYPES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    from pyspark.sql.functions import (
        row_number, rank, dense_rank, lag, lead,
        collect_list, collect_set, first, last,
        sum as spark_sum, avg, max as spark_max, min as spark_min
    )
    
    # Sample data with complex types
    window_schema = StructType([
        StructField("department", StringType(), True),
        StructField("employee", StructType([
            StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("salary", DoubleType(), True)
        ]), True),
        StructField("skills", ArrayType(StringType()), True),
        StructField("performance", MapType(StringType(), IntegerType()), True),
        StructField("year", IntegerType(), True)
    ])
    
    window_data = [
        ("IT", (101, "Alice", 75000.0), ["Python", "Spark"], {"Q1": 85, "Q2": 90}, 2023),
        ("IT", (102, "Bob", 82000.0), ["Java", "Kafka"], {"Q1": 88, "Q2": 92}, 2023),
        ("IT", (103, "Charlie", 68000.0), ["Python", "SQL"], {"Q1": 78, "Q2": 82}, 2023),
        ("HR", (201, "Diana", 65000.0), ["Communication"], {"Q1": 90, "Q2": 88}, 2023),
        ("HR", (202, "Eve", 70000.0), ["Recruiting"], {"Q1": 85, "Q2": 87}, 2023),
        ("IT", (101, "Alice", 78000.0), ["Python", "Spark", "ML"], {"Q1": 90, "Q2": 93}, 2024),
        ("IT", (102, "Bob", 85000.0), ["Java", "Kafka", "Cloud"], {"Q1": 89, "Q2": 91}, 2024),
    ]
    
    df_window = spark.createDataFrame(window_data, window_schema)
    
    print("\nOriginal Data:")
    df_window.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Window 1: Partition by department
    print("\nWindow 1: Ranking within Department:")
    window_dept = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("employee.salary").desc())
    
    df_ranked = df_window.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee.name").alias("name"),
        col("employee.salary").alias("salary"),
        row_number().over(window_dept).alias("row_num"),
        rank().over(window_dept).alias("rank"),
        dense_rank().over(window_dept).alias("dense_rank")
    )
    
    df_ranked.show()
    
    # Window 2: Collect complex types over window
    print("\nWindow 2: Collect Skills by Department:")
    window_dept_unbounded = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy("year").rowsBetween(
        Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.unboundedFollowing
    )
    
    df_collected = df_window.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee.name").alias("name"),
        col("year"),
        collect_list(col("employee.name")).over(window_dept_unbounded).alias("all_employees"),
        collect_set(flatten(collect_list(col("skills")).over(window_dept_unbounded))).alias("all_skills")
    )
    
    df_collected.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Window 3: Lag and Lead with struct types
    print("\nWindow 3: Salary Changes Over Time:")
    window_employee = Window.partitionBy("employee.id").orderBy("year")
    
    df_salary_change = df_window.select(
        col("employee.id").alias("emp_id"),
        col("employee.name").alias("name"),
        col("year"),
        col("employee.salary").alias("current_salary"),
        lag(col("employee.salary"), 1).over(window_employee).alias("previous_salary"),
        lead(col("employee.salary"), 1).over(window_employee).alias("next_salary")
    ).withColumn(
        "salary_increase",
        when(col("previous_salary").isNotNull(),
             col("current_salary") - col("previous_salary"))
        .otherwise(lit(0))
    )
    
    df_salary_change.show()
    
    # Window 4: Aggregate complex types
    print("\nWindow 4: Performance Aggregations:")
    
    # Extract performance scores and calculate averages
    df_performance = df_window.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee.name").alias("name"),
        col("year"),
        col("
```python
        col("performance")["Q1"].alias("q1_score"),
        col("performance")["Q2"].alias("q2_score"),
        ((col("performance")["Q1"] + col("performance")["Q2"]) / 2.0).alias("avg_score")
    )
    
    window_dept_year = Window.partitionBy("department", "year")
    
    df_perf_agg = df_performance.select(
        col("department"),
        col("name"),
        col("year"),
        col("avg_score"),
        avg(col("avg_score")).over(window_dept_year).alias("dept_avg_score"),
        spark_max(col("avg_score")).over(window_dept_year).alias("dept_max_score"),
        spark_min(col("avg_score")).over(window_dept_year).alias("dept_min_score")
    ).withColumn(
        "performance_vs_dept",
        col("avg_score") - col("dept_avg_score")
    )
    
    df_perf_agg.show()
    
    # Window 5: Running totals with arrays
    print("\nWindow 5: Skill Accumulation Over Time:")
    window_emp_time = Window.partitionBy("employee.id").orderBy("year").rowsBetween(
        Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow
    )
    
    df_skill_accumulation = df_window.select(
        col("employee.id").alias("emp_id"),
        col("employee.name").alias("name"),
        col("year"),
        col("skills"),
        flatten(collect_list(col("skills")).over(window_emp_time)).alias("accumulated_skills"),
        size(flatten(collect_list(col("skills")).over(window_emp_time))).alias("total_skills")
    )
    
    df_skill_accumulation.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Window 6: First and Last with complex types
    print("\nWindow 6: First and Last Values:")
    df_first_last = df_window.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee.name").alias("name"),
        col("year"),
        col("employee.salary").alias("salary"),
        first(col("employee.salary")).over(window_dept_unbounded).alias("first_salary_in_dept"),
        last(col("employee.salary")).over(window_dept_unbounded).alias("last_salary_in_dept"),
        first(struct(col("employee.name"), col("employee.salary"))).over(
            window_dept_unbounded
        ).alias("first_employee")
    )
    
    df_first_last.show(truncate=False)
    
    return df_window


# ============================================================================
# JOIN PATTERNS WITH COMPLEX TYPES
# ============================================================================

def join_patterns_with_complex_types():
    """
    Demonstrates join patterns involving complex data types.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("JOIN PATTERNS WITH COMPLEX TYPES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import col, explode, array_contains
    
    # Dataset 1: Users with complex profile
    users_schema = StructType([
        StructField("user_id", IntegerType(), False),
        StructField("profile", StructType([
            StructField("name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("email", StringType(), True),
            StructField("interests", ArrayType(StringType()), True)
        ]), True),
        StructField("metadata", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
    ])
    
    users_data = [
        (1, ("Alice", "alice@email.com", ["tech", "sports", "music"]), 
         {"tier": "gold", "region": "US"}),
        (2, ("Bob", "bob@email.com", ["tech", "gaming"]), 
         {"tier": "silver", "region": "EU"}),
        (3, ("Charlie", "charlie@email.com", ["music", "art"]), 
         {"tier": "bronze", "region": "US"})
    ]
    
    df_users = spark.createDataFrame(users_data, users_schema)
    
    # Dataset 2: Orders with nested items
    orders_schema = StructType([
        StructField("order_id", IntegerType(), False),
        StructField("user_id", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("items", ArrayType(StructType([
            StructField("product_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("product_name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("price", DoubleType(), True)
        ])), True),
        StructField("order_details", StructType([
            StructField("total_amount", DoubleType(), True),
            StructField("status", StringType(), True),
            StructField("shipping_address", StructType([
                StructField("city", StringType(), True),
                StructField("country", StringType(), True)
            ]), True)
        ]), True)
    ])
    
    orders_data = [
        (101, 1, 
         [(1, "Laptop", 1, 1200.0), (2, "Mouse", 2, 25.0)],
         (1250.0, "Delivered", ("New York", "USA"))),
        (102, 2,
         [(3, "Keyboard", 1, 80.0)],
         (80.0, "Shipped", ("London", "UK"))),
        (103, 1,
         [(4, "Monitor", 1, 350.0), (5, "Cable", 3, 10.0)],
         (380.0, "Processing", ("New York", "USA"))),
        (104, 3,
         [(6, "Headphones", 1, 150.0)],
         (150.0, "Delivered", ("Chicago", "USA")))
    ]
    
    df_orders = spark.createDataFrame(orders_data, orders_schema)
    
    print("\nUsers DataFrame:")
    df_users.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\nOrders DataFrame:")
    df_orders.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Join Pattern 1: Simple join with complex types
    print("\nJoin Pattern 1: Basic Join with Complex Types:")
    df_joined = df_users.join(df_orders, "user_id", "inner")
    
    df_joined.select(
        col("user_id"),
        col("profile.name").alias("customer_name"),
        col("order_id"),
        col("order_details.total_amount").alias("amount"),
        col("order_details.status").alias("status")
    ).show()
    
    # Join Pattern 2: Join with array explosion
    print("\nJoin Pattern 2: Join with Array Explosion:")
    df_order_items = df_orders.select(
        col("order_id"),
        col("user_id"),
        explode(col("items")).alias("item")
    ).select(
        "order_id",
        "user_id",
        "item.product_id",
        "item.product_name",
        "item.quantity",
        "item.price"
    )
    
    df_user_purchases = df_users.join(df_order_items, "user_id", "inner")
    
    df_user_purchases.select(
        col("user_id"),
        col("profile.name").alias("customer"),
        col("order_id"),
        col("product_name"),
        col("quantity"),
        col("price")
    ).show()
    
    # Join Pattern 3: Join with array contains condition
    print("\nJoin Pattern 3: Conditional Join on Array:")
    
    # Create products with categories
    products_data = [
        (1, "Laptop", ["tech", "electronics"]),
        (2, "Mouse", ["tech", "accessories"]),
        (3, "Keyboard", ["tech", "accessories"]),
        (4, "Monitor", ["tech", "electronics"]),
        (5, "Cable", ["tech", "accessories"]),
        (6, "Headphones", ["music", "electronics"])
    ]
    
    df_products = spark.createDataFrame(
        products_data, 
        ["product_id", "product_name", "categories"]
    )
    
    # Join users with products based on matching interests
    df_user_interests = df_users.select(
        col("user_id"),
        col("profile.name").alias("name"),
        explode(col("profile.interests")).alias("interest")
    )
    
    df_product_categories = df_products.select(
        col("product_id"),
        col("product_name"),
        explode(col("categories")).alias("category")
    )
    
    df_recommendations = df_user_interests.join(
        df_product_categories,
        df_user_interests.interest == df_product_categories.category,
        "inner"
    ).select(
        "user_id",
        "name",
        "product_id",
        "product_name",
        "interest"
    ).distinct()
    
    print("Product Recommendations based on User Interests:")
    df_recommendations.show()
    
    # Join Pattern 4: Join with map key matching
    print("\nJoin Pattern 4: Join with Map Matching:")
    
    # Create regions dataset
    regions_data = [
        ("US", "United States", "Americas"),
        ("EU", "European Union", "Europe"),
        ("UK", "United Kingdom", "Europe")
    ]
    
    df_regions = spark.createDataFrame(
        regions_data,
        ["region_code", "region_name", "continent"]
    )
    
    df_user_regions = df_users.select(
        col("user_id"),
        col("profile.name").alias("name"),
        col("metadata")["region"].alias("region_code")
    ).join(df_regions, "region_code", "left")
    
    df_user_regions.show()
    
    # Join Pattern 5: Nested struct join
    print("\nJoin Pattern 5: Join on Nested Struct Fields:")
    
    # Group orders by shipping city
    df_orders_by_city = df_orders.select(
        col("order_id"),
        col("user_id"),
        col("order_details.shipping_address.city").alias("city"),
        col("order_details.total_amount").alias("amount")
    )
    
    # Create city statistics
    city_stats_data = [
        ("New York", "USA", 8000000, "East"),
        ("London", "UK", 9000000, "Europe"),
        ("Chicago", "USA", 2700000, "Midwest")
    ]
    
    df_city_stats = spark.createDataFrame(
        city_stats_data,
        ["city", "country", "population", "zone"]
    )
    
    df_orders_with_city_info = df_orders_by_city.join(
        df_city_stats, "city", "left"
    )
    
    df_orders_with_city_info.show()
    
    # Join Pattern 6: Self-join with complex types
    print("\nJoin Pattern 6: Self-Join for User Similarities:")
    
    df_users_alias1 = df_users.alias("u1")
    df_users_alias2 = df_users.alias("u2")
    
    # Find users with common interests
    df_user1_interests = df_users_alias1.select(
        col("u1.user_id").alias("user1_id"),
        col("u1.profile.name").alias("user1_name"),
        explode(col("u1.profile.interests")).alias("interest")
    )
    
    df_user2_interests = df_users_alias2.select(
        col("u2.user_id").alias("user2_id"),
        col("u2.profile.name").alias("user2_name"),
        explode(col("u2.profile.interests")).alias("interest")
    )
    
    df_common_interests = df_user1_interests.join(
        df_user2_interests,
        (df_user1_interests.interest == df_user2_interests.interest) &
        (df_user1_interests.user1_id < df_user2_interests.user2_id),
        "inner"
    ).groupBy("user1_id", "user1_name", "user2_id", "user2_name").agg(
        collect_list("interest").alias("common_interests"),
        count("interest").alias("interest_count")
    )
    
    print("Users with Common Interests:")
    df_common_interests.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Join Pattern 7: Broadcast join with complex types
    print("\nJoin Pattern 7: Broadcast Join Optimization:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    # Small lookup table with complex structure
    tier_benefits_data = [
        ("gold", ["free_shipping", "priority_support", "exclusive_deals"], 20.0),
        ("silver", ["free_shipping", "priority_support"], 10.0),
        ("bronze", ["free_shipping"], 5.0)
    ]
    
    df_tier_benefits = spark.createDataFrame(
        tier_benefits_data,
        ["tier", "benefits", "discount_percent"]
    )
    
    df_user_benefits = df_users.select(
        col("user_id"),
        col("profile.name").alias("name"),
        col("metadata")["tier"].alias("tier")
    ).join(
        broadcast(df_tier_benefits),
        "tier",
        "left"
    )
    
    df_user_benefits.show(truncate=False)
    
    return df_joined


# ============================================================================
# AGGREGATION PATTERNS WITH COMPLEX TYPES
# ============================================================================

def aggregation_patterns_with_complex_types():
    """
    Demonstrates aggregation patterns with complex data types.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("AGGREGATION PATTERNS WITH COMPLEX TYPES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import (
        collect_list, collect_set, count, sum as spark_sum,
        avg, max as spark_max, min as spark_min, first, last,
        countDistinct, approx_count_distinct, struct, map_from_entries,
        flatten, array_distinct
    )
    
    # Sample data for aggregations
    agg_schema = StructType([
        StructField("department", StringType(), True),
        StructField("employee", StructType([
            StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("salary", DoubleType(), True),
            StructField("skills", ArrayType(StringType()), True)
        ]), True),
        StructField("projects", ArrayType(StructType([
            StructField("project_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("project_name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("hours", IntegerType(), True)
        ])), True),
        StructField("ratings", MapType(StringType(), IntegerType()), True)
    ])
    
    agg_data = [
        ("IT", (101, "Alice", 75000.0, ["Python", "Spark", "SQL"]),
         [(1, "Project A", 120), (2, "Project B", 80)],
         {"technical": 9, "communication": 8}),
        ("IT", (102, "Bob", 82000.0, ["Java", "Kafka", "SQL"]),
         [(1, "Project A", 100), (3, "Project C
```python
         [(1, "Project A", 100), (3, "Project C", 150)],
         {"technical": 8, "communication": 9}),
        ("IT", (103, "Charlie", 68000.0, ["Python", "SQL", "Docker"]),
         [(2, "Project B", 90)],
         {"technical": 7, "communication": 7}),
        ("HR", (201, "Diana", 65000.0, ["Recruiting", "Communication"]),
         [(4, "Project D", 110)],
         {"technical": 6, "communication": 9}),
        ("HR", (202, "Eve", 70000.0, ["Training", "Communication"]),
         [(4, "Project D", 130), (5, "Project E", 95)],
         {"technical": 7, "communication": 10}),
        ("Finance", (301, "Frank", 90000.0, ["Excel", "SAP", "Analysis"]),
         [(6, "Project F", 140)],
         {"technical": 8, "communication": 7})
    ]
    
    df_agg = spark.createDataFrame(agg_data, agg_schema)
    
    print("\nOriginal Data:")
    df_agg.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 1: Basic aggregations with struct fields
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 1: Basic Aggregations on Struct Fields:")
    df_basic_agg = df_agg.groupBy("department").agg(
        count("*").alias("employee_count"),
        avg(col("employee.salary")).alias("avg_salary"),
        spark_max(col("employee.salary")).alias("max_salary"),
        spark_min(col("employee.salary")).alias("min_salary"),
        spark_sum(col("employee.salary")).alias("total_salary")
    )
    
    df_basic_agg.show()
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 2: Collect complex types
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 2: Collecting Complex Types:")
    df_collect_agg = df_agg.groupBy("department").agg(
        collect_list(col("employee.name")).alias("employee_names"),
        collect_list(col("employee")).alias("all_employees"),
        collect_set(col("employee.name")).alias("unique_names"),
        first(col("employee")).alias("first_employee"),
        last(col("employee")).alias("last_employee")
    )
    
    df_collect_agg.show(truncate=False)
    df_collect_agg.printSchema()
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 3: Aggregating arrays
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 3: Aggregating Arrays:")
    df_array_agg = df_agg.groupBy("department").agg(
        collect_list(col("employee.skills")).alias("all_skills_nested"),
        flatten(collect_list(col("employee.skills"))).alias("all_skills_flat"),
        array_distinct(flatten(collect_list(col("employee.skills")))).alias("unique_skills")
    )
    
    df_array_agg.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Count unique skills per department
    print("\nSkill Count per Department:")
    df_skill_count = df_array_agg.select(
        col("department"),
        size(col("unique_skills")).alias("unique_skill_count"),
        col("unique_skills")
    )
    
    df_skill_count.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 4: Aggregating nested arrays (projects)
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 4: Aggregating Nested Arrays:")
    
    # First explode projects, then aggregate
    df_projects_exploded = df_agg.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee.name").alias("employee_name"),
        explode(col("projects")).alias("project")
    ).select(
        "department",
        "employee_name",
        "project.project_id",
        "project.project_name",
        "project.hours"
    )
    
    print("Exploded Projects:")
    df_projects_exploded.show()
    
    # Aggregate project hours by department
    df_project_agg = df_projects_exploded.groupBy("department").agg(
        spark_sum("hours").alias("total_hours"),
        avg("hours").alias("avg_hours_per_project"),
        countDistinct("project_id").alias("unique_projects"),
        collect_set("project_name").alias("project_names")
    )
    
    df_project_agg.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 5: Aggregating maps
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 5: Aggregating Map Types:")
    
    # Extract map values and aggregate
    df_ratings_exploded = df_agg.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee.name").alias("employee_name"),
        explode(col("ratings")).alias("rating_type", "rating_value")
    )
    
    print("Exploded Ratings:")
    df_ratings_exploded.show()
    
    df_ratings_agg = df_ratings_exploded.groupBy("department", "rating_type").agg(
        avg("rating_value").alias("avg_rating"),
        spark_max("rating_value").alias("max_rating"),
        spark_min("rating_value").alias("min_rating")
    )
    
    df_ratings_agg.show()
    
    # Pivot ratings by type
    print("\nPivoted Ratings by Department:")
    df_ratings_pivot = df_ratings_exploded.groupBy("department").pivot("rating_type").agg(
        avg("rating_value")
    )
    
    df_ratings_pivot.show()
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 6: Creating complex aggregated structures
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 6: Creating Complex Aggregated Structures:")
    df_complex_agg = df_agg.groupBy("department").agg(
        struct(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            avg(col("employee.salary")).alias("avg_salary"),
            collect_list(col("employee.name")).alias("employees")
        ).alias("department_stats"),
        struct(
            array_distinct(flatten(collect_list(col("employee.skills")))).alias("all_skills"),
            size(array_distinct(flatten(collect_list(col("employee.skills"))))).alias("skill_count")
        ).alias("skill_stats")
    )
    
    df_complex_agg.show(truncate=False)
    df_complex_agg.printSchema()
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 7: Multi-level aggregations
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 7: Multi-level Aggregations:")
    
    # First level: aggregate by department and employee
    df_employee_project_agg = df_agg.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee.id").alias("emp_id"),
        col("employee.name").alias("emp_name"),
        explode(col("projects")).alias("project")
    ).groupBy("department", "emp_id", "emp_name").agg(
        spark_sum("project.hours").alias("total_hours"),
        count("project.project_id").alias("project_count")
    )
    
    print("Employee-level Aggregation:")
    df_employee_project_agg.show()
    
    # Second level: aggregate by department
    df_dept_summary = df_employee_project_agg.groupBy("department").agg(
        count("emp_id").alias("employee_count"),
        spark_sum("total_hours").alias("dept_total_hours"),
        avg("total_hours").alias("avg_hours_per_employee"),
        collect_list(
            struct(
                col("emp_name"),
                col("total_hours"),
                col("project_count")
            )
        ).alias("employee_details")
    )
    
    print("Department-level Summary:")
    df_dept_summary.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 8: Conditional aggregations with complex types
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 8: Conditional Aggregations:")
    df_conditional_agg = df_agg.groupBy("department").agg(
        count(when(col("employee.salary") > 70000, 1)).alias("high_earners"),
        count(when(col("employee.salary") <= 70000, 1)).alias("normal_earners"),
        avg(when(col("employee.salary") > 70000, col("employee.salary"))).alias("avg_high_salary"),
        collect_list(
            when(col("employee.salary") > 70000, col("employee.name"))
        ).alias("high_earner_names")
    )
    
    df_conditional_agg.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 9: Creating map from aggregated data
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 9: Creating Map from Aggregations:")
    
    # Aggregate ratings into a map structure
    df_rating_map = df_ratings_exploded.groupBy("department").agg(
        map_from_entries(
            collect_list(
                struct(
                    col("rating_type").alias("key"),
                    col("rating_value").cast(StringType()).alias("value")
                )
            )
        ).alias("rating_map")
    )
    
    df_rating_map.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Aggregation Pattern 10: Comprehensive aggregation summary
    print("\nAggregation Pattern 10: Comprehensive Department Summary:")
    df_comprehensive = df_agg.groupBy("department").agg(
        struct(
            # Employee statistics
            count("*").alias("total_employees"),
            avg(col("employee.salary")).alias("avg_salary"),
            spark_sum(col("employee.salary")).alias("total_payroll"),
            collect_list(
                struct(
                    col("employee.id").alias("id"),
                    col("employee.name").alias("name"),
                    col("employee.salary").alias("salary")
                )
            ).alias("employee_list")
        ).alias("employee_stats"),
        struct(
            # Skill statistics
            array_distinct(flatten(collect_list(col("employee.skills")))).alias("unique_skills"),
            size(array_distinct(flatten(collect_list(col("employee.skills"))))).alias("skill_diversity"),
            flatten(collect_list(col("employee.skills"))).alias("all_skills")
        ).alias("skill_stats"),
        struct(
            # Project statistics
            size(flatten(collect_list(col("projects")))).alias("total_project_assignments"),
            countDistinct(flatten(collect_list(col("projects.project_id")))).alias("unique_projects")
        ).alias("project_stats")
    )
    
    df_comprehensive.show(truncate=False)
    df_comprehensive.printSchema()
    
    # Access nested aggregated data
    print("\nAccessing Nested Aggregated Data:")
    df_comprehensive.select(
        col("department"),
        col("employee_stats.total_employees"),
        col("employee_stats.avg_salary"),
        col("skill_stats.skill_diversity"),
        col("project_stats.unique_projects")
    ).show()
    
    return df_agg


# ============================================================================
# ERROR HANDLING AND EDGE CASES
# ============================================================================

def error_handling_patterns():
    """
    Demonstrates error handling and edge case management for complex types.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ERROR HANDLING AND EDGE CASES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import (
        when, col, isnull, size, coalesce, 
        array, lit, struct, create_map
    )
    
    # Create data with various edge cases
    edge_case_schema = StructType([
        StructField("id", IntegerType(), False),
        StructField("name", StringType(), True),
        StructField("data", StructType([
            StructField("value", StringType(), True),
            StructField("count", IntegerType(), True)
        ]), True),
        StructField("tags", ArrayType(StringType()), True),
        StructField("metadata", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
    ])
    
    edge_case_data = [
        (1, "Normal", ("value1", 10), ["tag1", "tag2"], {"key1": "val1"}),
        (2, "Null Struct", None, ["tag3"], {"key2": "val2"}),
        (3, "Empty Array", ("value2", 20), [], {"key3": "val3"}),
        (4, "Null Array", ("value3", 30), None, {"key4": "val4"}),
        (5, "Empty Map", ("value4", 40), ["tag4"], {}),
        (6, "Null Map", ("value5", 50), ["tag5"], None),
        (7, "All Nulls", None, None, None),
        (8, "Partial Nulls", ("value6", None), ["tag6", None], {"key5": None})
    ]
    
    df_edge = spark.createDataFrame(edge_case_data, edge_case_schema)
    
    print("\nData with Edge Cases:")
    df_edge.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 1: Handling null structs
    print("\nPattern 1: Handling Null Structs:")
    df_struct_handling = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        col("data"),
        when(col("data").isNull(), lit("Struct is null"))
            .otherwise(lit("Struct exists")).alias("struct_status"),
        coalesce(col("data.value"), lit("N/A")).alias("safe_value"),
        coalesce(col("data.count"), lit(0)).alias("safe_count")
    )
    
    df_struct_handling.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 2: Handling null/empty arrays
    print("\nPattern 2: Handling Null/Empty Arrays:")
    df_array_handling = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        col("tags"),
        when(col("tags").isNull(), lit("Null"))
            .when(size(col("tags")) == 0, lit("Empty"))
            .otherwise(lit("Has Data")).alias("array_status"),
        coalesce(col("tags"), array()).alias("safe_tags"),
        coalesce(size(col("tags")), lit(0)).alias("tag_count")
    )
    
    df_array_handling.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 3: Handling null/empty maps
    print("\nPattern 3: Handling Null/Empty Maps:")
    df_map_handling = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        col("metadata"),
        when(col("metadata").isNull(), lit("Null"))
            .when(size(col("metadata")) == 0, lit("Empty"))
            .otherwise(lit("Has Data")).alias("map_status"),
        coalesce(size(col("metadata")), lit(0)).alias("metadata_count"),
        coalesce(col("metadata")["key1"], lit("default")).alias("safe_key_access")
    )
    
    df_map_handling.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 4: Providing default complex values
    print("\nPattern 4: Providing Default Complex Values:")
    df_defaults = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        coalesce(
            col("data"),
            struct(lit("default").alias("value"), lit
```python
            struct(lit("default").alias("value"), lit(0).alias("count"))
        ).alias("data_with_default"),
        coalesce(
            col("tags"),
            array(lit("default_tag"))
        ).alias("tags_with_default"),
        coalesce(
            col("metadata"),
            create_map(lit("default_key"), lit("default_value"))
        ).alias("metadata_with_default")
    )
    
    df_defaults.show(truncate=False)
    df_defaults.printSchema()
    
    # Pattern 5: Safe array operations
    print("\nPattern 5: Safe Array Operations:")
    df_safe_array = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        col("tags"),
        when(col("tags").isNotNull() & (size(col("tags")) > 0),
             col("tags")[0]).otherwise(lit("N/A")).alias("first_tag_safe"),
        when(col("tags").isNotNull(),
             array_contains(col("tags"), "tag1")).otherwise(lit(False)).alias("contains_tag1"),
        when(col("tags").isNotNull(),
             size(col("tags"))).otherwise(lit(0)).alias("safe_size")
    )
    
    df_safe_array.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 6: Safe map operations
    print("\nPattern 6: Safe Map Operations:")
    df_safe_map = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        col("metadata"),
        when(col("metadata").isNotNull(),
             map_keys(col("metadata"))).otherwise(array()).alias("safe_keys"),
        when(col("metadata").isNotNull(),
             map_values(col("metadata"))).otherwise(array()).alias("safe_values"),
        when(col("metadata").isNotNull() & (size(col("metadata")) > 0),
             element_at(map_keys(col("metadata")), 1)).otherwise(lit("N/A")).alias("first_key")
    )
    
    df_safe_map.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 7: Handling null values in nested structures
    print("\nPattern 7: Handling Nulls in Nested Structures:")
    df_nested_nulls = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        when(col("data").isNotNull(),
             when(col("data.value").isNotNull(), col("data.value"))
             .otherwise(lit("value_is_null"))
        ).otherwise(lit("struct_is_null")).alias("nested_value_handling"),
        when(col("data").isNotNull(),
             when(col("data.count").isNotNull(), col("data.count"))
             .otherwise(lit(-1))
        ).otherwise(lit(-999)).alias("nested_count_handling")
    )
    
    df_nested_nulls.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 8: Try-catch pattern using when/otherwise
    print("\nPattern 8: Validation and Error Reporting:")
    df_validation_report = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        struct(
            when(col("data").isNull(), lit("ERROR: Struct is null"))
                .when(col("data.value").isNull(), lit("WARNING: Value is null"))
                .otherwise(lit("OK")).alias("data_status"),
            when(col("tags").isNull(), lit("ERROR: Array is null"))
                .when(size(col("tags")) == 0, lit("WARNING: Array is empty"))
                .otherwise(lit("OK")).alias("tags_status"),
            when(col("metadata").isNull(), lit("ERROR: Map is null"))
                .when(size(col("metadata")) == 0, lit("WARNING: Map is empty"))
                .otherwise(lit("OK")).alias("metadata_status")
        ).alias("validation_report")
    )
    
    df_validation_report.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 9: Filtering out invalid records
    print("\nPattern 9: Filtering Invalid Records:")
    df_valid_only = df_edge.filter(
        col("data").isNotNull() &
        col("tags").isNotNull() &
        (size(col("tags")) > 0) &
        col("metadata").isNotNull() &
        (size(col("metadata")) > 0)
    )
    
    print("Valid Records Only:")
    df_valid_only.show(truncate=False)
    
    print(f"Original count: {df_edge.count()}")
    print(f"Valid count: {df_valid_only.count()}")
    print(f"Invalid count: {df_edge.count() - df_valid_only.count()}")
    
    # Pattern 10: Creating error report
    print("\nPattern 10: Comprehensive Error Report:")
    df_error_report = df_edge.select(
        col("id"),
        col("name"),
        struct(
            col("data").isNull().alias("data_is_null"),
            when(col("data").isNotNull(), col("data.value").isNull()).otherwise(lit(False)).alias("data_value_is_null"),
            col("tags").isNull().alias("tags_is_null"),
            when(col("tags").isNotNull(), size(col("tags")) == 0).otherwise(lit(False)).alias("tags_is_empty"),
            col("metadata").isNull().alias("metadata_is_null"),
            when(col("metadata").isNotNull(), size(col("metadata")) == 0).otherwise(lit(False)).alias("metadata_is_empty")
        ).alias("null_checks"),
        when(
            col("data").isNull() | col("tags").isNull() | col("metadata").isNull() |
            (size(col("tags")) == 0) | (size(col("metadata")) == 0),
            lit("HAS_ISSUES")
        ).otherwise(lit("CLEAN")).alias("record_status")
    )
    
    df_error_report.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Summary statistics
    print("\nError Summary:")
    df_error_report.groupBy("record_status").count().show()
    
    return df_edge

def real_world_ecommerce_example():
    """
    Comprehensive real-world example: E-commerce analytics with all type patterns.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("REAL-WORLD USE CASE: E-COMMERCE ANALYTICS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import (
        col, explode, struct, array, when, sum as spark_sum,
        avg, count, countDistinct, collect_list, window, 
        date_format, dayofweek, hour, to_date
    )
    
    # Define comprehensive e-commerce schema
    ecommerce_schema = StructType([
        StructField("transaction_id", LongType(), False),
        StructField("timestamp", TimestampType(), False),
        StructField("customer", StructType([
            StructField("customer_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("email", StringType(), True),
            StructField("segment", StringType(), True),
            StructField("lifetime_value", DoubleType(), True),
            StructField("preferences", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
        ]), True),
        StructField("items", ArrayType(StructType([
            StructField("sku", StringType(), True),
            StructField("product_name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("category", StringType(), True),
            StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("unit_price", DoubleType(), True),
            StructField("discount", DoubleType(), True),
            StructField("attributes", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
        ])), True),
        StructField("payment", StructType([
            StructField("method", StringType(), True),
            StructField("card_type", StringType(), True),
            StructField("installments", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("status", StringType(), True)
        ]), True),
        StructField("shipping", StructType([
            StructField("address", StructType([
                StructField("street", StringType(), True),
                StructField("city", StringType(), True),
                StructField("state", StringType(), True),
                StructField("zipcode", StringType(), True),
                StructField("country", StringType(), True)
            ]), True),
            StructField("method", StringType(), True),
            StructField("cost", DoubleType(), True)
        ]), True),
        StructField("metadata", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
    ])
    
    # Generate sample e-commerce data
    ecommerce_data = [
        (1001, datetime(2024, 1, 15, 10, 30, 0),
         (101, "Alice Johnson", "alice@email.com", "Premium", 5000.0, 
          {"newsletter": "yes", "sms": "no"}),
         [
             ("SKU001", "Laptop Pro 15", "Electronics", 1, 1299.99, 100.0, 
              {"brand": "TechCorp", "warranty": "2years"}),
             ("SKU002", "Wireless Mouse", "Accessories", 2, 29.99, 5.0,
              {"brand": "TechCorp", "color": "black"})
         ],
         ("credit_card", "Visa", 1, "completed"),
         (("123 Main St", "New York", "NY", "10001", "USA"), 
          "express", 15.99),
         {"device": "mobile", "app_version": "2.1.0"}),
        
        (1002, datetime(2024, 1, 15, 11, 45, 0),
         (102, "Bob Smith", "bob@email.com", "Standard", 2000.0,
          {"newsletter": "yes", "sms": "yes"}),
         [
             ("SKU003", "Smartphone X", "Electronics", 1, 899.99, 50.0,
              {"brand": "PhoneCo", "storage": "128GB"}),
             ("SKU004", "Phone Case", "Accessories", 1, 19.99, 0.0,
              {"brand": "Generic", "color": "blue"}),
             ("SKU005", "Screen Protector", "Accessories", 2, 9.99, 2.0,
              {"brand": "Generic", "type": "tempered_glass"})
         ],
         ("paypal", None, 1, "completed"),
         (("456 Oak Ave", "Los Angeles", "CA", "90001", "USA"),
          "standard", 5.99),
         {"device": "desktop", "browser": "chrome"}),
        
        (1003, datetime(2024, 1, 15, 14, 20, 0),
         (103, "Carol White", "carol@email.com", "Premium", 8000.0,
          {"newsletter": "no", "sms": "yes"}),
         [
             ("SKU006", "4K Monitor", "Electronics", 2, 449.99, 50.0,
              {"brand": "DisplayTech", "size": "27inch"}),
             ("SKU007", "HDMI Cable", "Accessories", 2, 12.99, 0.0,
              {"brand": "Generic", "length": "6ft"})
         ],
         ("credit_card", "Mastercard", 3, "completed"),
         (("789 Pine Rd", "Chicago", "IL", "60601", "USA"),
          "express", 15.99),
         {"device": "mobile", "app_version": "2.1.0"}),
        
        (1004, datetime(2024, 1, 16, 9, 15, 0),
         (101, "Alice Johnson", "alice@email.com", "Premium", 5000.0,
          {"newsletter": "yes", "sms": "no"}),
         [
             ("SKU008", "Mechanical Keyboard", "Accessories", 1, 129.99, 15.0,
              {"brand": "KeyMaster", "switches": "cherry_mx"})
         ],
         ("credit_card", "Visa", 1, "completed"),
         (("123 Main St", "New York", "NY", "10001", "USA"),
          "standard", 5.99),
         {"device": "desktop", "browser": "firefox"})
    ]
    
    df_ecommerce = spark.createDataFrame(ecommerce_data, ecommerce_schema)
    
    print("\nE-Commerce Transactions:")
    df_ecommerce.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Analysis 1: Customer Segmentation Analysis
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 1: Customer Segmentation Analysis")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_customer_analysis = df_ecommerce.groupBy(
        col("customer.segment")
    ).agg(
        countDistinct(col("customer.customer_id")).alias("unique_customers"),
        count("*").alias("total_transactions"),
        avg(col("customer.lifetime_value")).alias("avg_lifetime_value"),
        collect_set(col("customer.name")).alias("customers")
    )
    
    df_customer_analysis.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Analysis 2: Product Category Performance
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 2: Product Category Performance")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_items_exploded = df_ecommerce.select(
        col("transaction_id"),
        col("timestamp"),
        col("customer.segment").alias("customer_segment"),
        explode(col("items")).alias("item")
    ).select(
        "transaction_id",
        "timestamp",
        "customer_segment",
        "item.category",
        "item.product_name",
        "item.quantity",
        "item.unit_price",
        "item.discount",
        (col("item.quantity") * col("item.unit_price") - col("item.discount")).alias("item_revenue")
    )
    
    df_category_performance = df_items_exploded.groupBy("category").agg(
        count("*").alias("items_sold"),
        spark_sum("quantity").alias("total_quantity"),
        spark_sum("item_revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
        avg("item_revenue").alias("avg_revenue_per_item"),
        countDistinct("product_name").alias("unique_products")
    ).orderBy(col("total_revenue").desc())
    
    df_category_performance.show()
    
    # Analysis 3: Transaction Value Analysis
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 3: Transaction Value Analysis")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_transaction_value = df_ecommerce.select(
        col("transaction_id"),
        col("timestamp"),
        col("customer.name").alias("customer"),
        col("customer.segment").alias("segment"),
        col("items"),
        col("shipping.cost").alias("shipping_cost")
    ).withColumn(
        "item_total",
        aggregate(
            col("items"),
            lit(0.0),
            lambda acc, x: acc + (x.quantity * x.unit_price - x.discount)
        )
    ).withColumn(
        "total_discount",
        aggregate(
            col("items"),
            lit(0.0),
            lambda acc, x: acc
```python
            lambda acc, x: acc + x.discount
        )
    ).withColumn(
        "final_total",
        col("item_total") + col("shipping_cost")
    )
    
    df_transaction_value.select(
        "transaction_id",
        "customer",
        "segment",
        "item_total",
        "total_discount",
        "shipping_cost",
        "final_total"
    ).show()
    
    # Summary statistics
    print("\nTransaction Value Summary:")
    df_transaction_value.groupBy("segment").agg(
        count("*").alias("transactions"),
        avg("final_total").alias("avg_transaction_value"),
        spark_sum("final_total").alias("total_revenue"),
        avg("total_discount").alias("avg_discount")
    ).show()
    
    # Analysis 4: Payment Method Analysis
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 4: Payment Method Analysis")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_payment_analysis = df_ecommerce.groupBy(
        col("payment.method"),
        col("payment.status")
    ).agg(
        count("*").alias("transaction_count"),
        countDistinct(col("customer.customer_id")).alias("unique_customers")
    )
    
    df_payment_analysis.show()
    
    # Analysis 5: Geographic Analysis
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 5: Geographic Analysis")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_geographic = df_ecommerce.groupBy(
        col("shipping.address.state"),
        col("shipping.address.city")
    ).agg(
        count("*").alias("order_count"),
        countDistinct(col("customer.customer_id")).alias("unique_customers"),
        avg(col("shipping.cost")).alias("avg_shipping_cost"),
        collect_set(col("shipping.method")).alias("shipping_methods_used")
    ).orderBy(col("order_count").desc())
    
    df_geographic.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Analysis 6: Time-based Analysis
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 6: Time-based Analysis")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_temporal = df_ecommerce.select(
        col("transaction_id"),
        to_date(col("timestamp")).alias("date"),
        date_format(col("timestamp"), "EEEE").alias("day_of_week"),
        hour(col("timestamp")).alias("hour_of_day"),
        col("customer.segment").alias("segment")
    )
    
    print("Transactions by Day of Week:")
    df_temporal.groupBy("day_of_week").agg(
        count("*").alias("transaction_count")
    ).orderBy("transaction_count", ascending=False).show()
    
    print("\nTransactions by Hour of Day:")
    df_temporal.groupBy("hour_of_day").agg(
        count("*").alias("transaction_count")
    ).orderBy("hour_of_day").show()
    
    # Analysis 7: Customer Behavior Analysis
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 7: Customer Behavior Analysis")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_customer_behavior = df_ecommerce.groupBy(
        col("customer.customer_id"),
        col("customer.name"),
        col("customer.segment")
    ).agg(
        count("*").alias("purchase_count"),
        countDistinct(to_date(col("timestamp"))).alias("unique_purchase_days"),
        collect_list(
            struct(
                col("transaction_id"),
                to_date(col("timestamp")).alias("date"),
                size(col("items")).alias("items_count")
            )
        ).alias("purchase_history")
    )
    
    df_customer_behavior.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Analysis 8: Product Affinity Analysis
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 8: Product Affinity Analysis (Items Bought Together)")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Get transactions with multiple items
    df_multi_item = df_ecommerce.filter(size(col("items")) > 1).select(
        col("transaction_id"),
        col("items")
    )
    
    # Explode to get all item combinations
    df_item_pairs = df_multi_item.select(
        col("transaction_id"),
        explode(col("items")).alias("item1")
    ).alias("t1").join(
        df_multi_item.select(
            col("transaction_id"),
            explode(col("items")).alias("item2")
        ).alias("t2"),
        col("t1.transaction_id") == col("t2.transaction_id"),
        "inner"
    ).filter(
        col("t1.item1.sku") < col("t2.item2.sku")
    ).select(
        col("t1.item1.product_name").alias("product1"),
        col("t2.item2.product_name").alias("product2"),
        col("t1.item1.category").alias("category1"),
        col("t2.item2.category").alias("category2")
    ).groupBy("product1", "product2").agg(
        count("*").alias("times_bought_together")
    ).orderBy(col("times_bought_together").desc())
    
    print("Products Frequently Bought Together:")
    df_item_pairs.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Analysis 9: Discount Effectiveness
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 9: Discount Effectiveness Analysis")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_discount_analysis = df_items_exploded.withColumn(
        "discount_rate",
        when(col("item.unit_price") > 0,
             (col("item.discount") / (col("item.quantity") * col("item.unit_price"))) * 100
        ).otherwise(0)
    ).groupBy("category").agg(
        count("*").alias("item_count"),
        avg("discount_rate").alias("avg_discount_rate"),
        spark_sum("item.discount").alias("total_discount_given"),
        spark_sum("item_revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
        (spark_sum("item.discount") / spark_sum("item_revenue") * 100).alias("discount_to_revenue_ratio")
    )
    
    df_discount_analysis.show()
    
    # Analysis 10: Customer Lifetime Value Prediction Features
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 10: Customer Features for LTV Prediction")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_customer_features = df_ecommerce.groupBy(
        col("customer.customer_id"),
        col("customer.name"),
        col("customer.segment"),
        col("customer.lifetime_value")
    ).agg(
        # Transaction features
        count("*").alias("total_transactions"),
        countDistinct(to_date(col("timestamp"))).alias("active_days"),
        
        # Product features
        avg(size(col("items"))).alias("avg_items_per_transaction"),
        countDistinct(flatten(collect_list(col("items.category")))).alias("unique_categories"),
        
        # Payment features
        collect_set(col("payment.method")).alias("payment_methods_used"),
        avg(col("payment.installments")).alias("avg_installments"),
        
        # Shipping features
        avg(col("shipping.cost")).alias("avg_shipping_cost"),
        collect_set(col("shipping.method")).alias("shipping_methods_used"),
        
        # Device features
        collect_set(col("metadata")["device"]).alias("devices_used"),
        
        # Preference features
        first(col("customer.preferences")).alias("preferences")
    )
    
    df_customer_features.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Analysis 11: Comprehensive Business Dashboard Data
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ANALYSIS 11: Comprehensive Business Dashboard")
    print("="*80)
    
    df_dashboard = df_ecommerce.agg(
        struct(
            # Overall metrics
            count("*").alias("total_transactions"),
            countDistinct(col("customer.customer_id")).alias("unique_customers"),
            countDistinct(to_date(col("timestamp"))).alias("active_days"),
            
            # Revenue metrics
            spark_sum(
                aggregate(
                    col("items"),
                    lit(0.0),
                    lambda acc, x: acc + (x.quantity * x.unit_price - x.discount)
                ) + col("shipping.cost")
            ).alias("total_revenue"),
            
            avg(
                aggregate(
                    col("items"),
                    lit(0.0),
                    lambda acc, x: acc + (x.quantity * x.unit_price - x.discount)
                ) + col("shipping.cost")
            ).alias("avg_order_value")
        ).alias("overall_metrics"),
        
        struct(
            # Product metrics
            spark_sum(
                aggregate(
                    col("items"),
                    lit(0),
                    lambda acc, x: acc + x.quantity
                )
            ).alias("total_items_sold"),
            
            avg(size(col("items"))).alias("avg_items_per_order"),
            
            countDistinct(flatten(collect_list(col("items.sku")))).alias("unique_skus_sold")
        ).alias("product_metrics"),
        
        struct(
            # Customer metrics
            avg(col("customer.lifetime_value")).alias("avg_customer_ltv"),
            collect_set(col("customer.segment")).alias("segments"),
            countDistinct(col("customer.email")).alias("unique_emails")
        ).alias("customer_metrics"),
        
        struct(
            # Geographic metrics
            countDistinct(col("shipping.address.state")).alias("states_served"),
            countDistinct(col("shipping.address.city")).alias("cities_served"),
            avg(col("shipping.cost")).alias("avg_shipping_cost")
        ).alias("geographic_metrics")
    )
    
    df_dashboard.show(truncate=False)
    df_dashboard.printSchema()
    
    # Extract and display dashboard metrics
    print("\nDashboard Metrics Summary:")
    df_dashboard.select(
        col("overall_metrics.total_transactions"),
        col("overall_metrics.unique_customers"),
        col("overall_metrics.total_revenue"),
        col("overall_metrics.avg_order_value"),
        col("product_metrics.total_items_sold"),
        col("customer_metrics.avg_customer_ltv")
    ).show()
    
    return df_ecommerce

    summary_text = """
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                    PYSPARK DATA TYPE PATTERNS SUMMARY                      ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 1. PRIMITIVE TYPE PATTERN                                                  │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Basic data types: Integer, String, Double, Boolean, Date, Timestamp     │
    │ • Use for: Simple atomic values, filtering, aggregations                  │
    │ • Best for: Performance-critical operations, join keys                    │
    │ • Example: customer_id (IntegerType), email (StringType)                  │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 2. COMPLEX TYPE PATTERN                                                    │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Types: ArrayType, MapType, StructType                                   │
    │ • Use for: Multi-dimensional data, collections                            │
    │ • Best for: Reducing column count, related data grouping                  │
    │ • Example: skills (ArrayType), metadata (MapType)                         │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 3. COMPOSITE TYPE PATTERN                                                  │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Combination of multiple complex types                                   │
    │ • Use for: Hierarchical business entities                                 │
    │ • Best for: Order systems, user profiles, nested documents                │
    │ • Example: Order with items (Array of Structs)                            │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 4. USER-DEFINED TYPE PATTERN                                               │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Reusable type definitions for domain modeling                           │
    │ • Use for: Consistent schema across datasets                              │
    │ • Best for: Enterprise applications, data standardization                 │
    │ • Example: AddressType, ContactType reused across tables                  │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 5. NESTED TYPE PATTERN                                                     │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Deep hierarchical structures (3-4 levels max recommended)               │
    │ • Use for: JSON data, tree structures, organizational hierarchies         │
    │ • Best for: Document databases, complex business domains                  │
    │ • Warning: Can impact performance if too deep                             │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 6. ARRAY TYPE PATTERN                                                      │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Ordered collections of same-type elements                               │
    │ • Use for: Lists, sequences, tags, time series                            │
    │ • Operations: explode, array_contains, array_distinct, flatten            │
    │ • Best for: Variable-length collections with order                        │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 7. MAP TYPE PATTERN                                                        │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Key-value pairs for dynamic attributes                                  │
    │
```python
    │ • Use for: Metadata, dynamic properties, sparse data                      │
    │ • Operations: map_keys, map_values, element_at, map_filter                │
    │ • Best for: Unknown or varying attribute sets                             │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 8. STRUCT TYPE PATTERN                                                     │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ • Fixed set of named fields (like a record/row)                           │

    │ • Best for: Known schema, type safety, better performance than maps       │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                           BEST PRACTICES GUIDE                             ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ SCHEMA DESIGN                                                              ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
    
    ✓ Define schemas explicitly for better performance and type safety
    ✓ Use nullable=False for required fields
    ✓ Choose appropriate precision (Int vs Long, Float vs Double)
    ✓ Limit nesting depth to 3-4 levels maximum
    ✓ Use Struct over Map when schema is known
    ✓ Document complex type structures
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION                                                   ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
    
    ✓ Project only needed fields early: select("struct.field") vs select("struct")
    ✓ Use primitive types for partition keys and join conditions
    ✓ Cache DataFrames with complex types if reused multiple times
    ✓ Avoid repeated explode operations - explode once and cache
    ✓ Use broadcast joins for small lookup tables
    ✓ Flatten nested structures in hot code paths
    ✓ Use array_distinct before operations on large arrays
    ✓ Consider columnar format (Parquet) for nested data
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ DATA QUALITY & VALIDATION                                                  ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
    
    ✓ Always check for null values in complex types
    ✓ Use coalesce() to provide default values
    ✓ Validate array sizes before accessing elements
    ✓ Check map key existence before access
    ✓ Use when/otherwise for safe type conversions
    ✓ Implement data quality checks at ingestion
    ✓ Create validation reports for monitoring
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ ARRAY OPERATIONS                                                           ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
    
    ✓ Use array_contains for membership checks
    ✓ Use array_distinct to remove duplicates
    ✓ Use flatten for nested arrays
    ✓ Use size() to get array length
    ✓ Explode carefully - it multiplies rows
    ✓ Use collect_list/collect_set for aggregations
    ✓ Consider array size limits (avoid very large arrays)
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ MAP OPERATIONS                                                             ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
    
    ✓ Use map_keys() and map_values() to extract components
    ✓ Use element_at() for safe key access
    ✓ Check map size before operations
    ✓ Use map_from_arrays to create maps dynamically
    ✓ Prefer Struct over Map when schema is fixed
    ✓ Use explode for map iteration
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ STRUCT OPERATIONS                                                          ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
    
    ✓ Use dot notation for field access: col("struct.field")
    ✓ Use select("struct.*") to flatten all fields
    ✓ Use struct() to create structs dynamically
    ✓ Validate struct is not null before accessing fields
    ✓ Use withColumn to update struct fields
    ✓ Better performance than maps for known schemas
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ SCHEMA EVOLUTION                                                           ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛
    
    ✓ Add new fields as nullable for backward compatibility
    ✓ Use coalesce for default values in evolved schemas
    ✓ Version your schemas in metadata
    ✓ Test schema compatibility before deployment
    ✓ Document schema changes
    ✓ Use Delta Lake for ACID transactions and schema evolution
    
    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
    ┃ SERIALIZATION & STORAGE                                                    ┃
    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

def create_sample_data():

    orders_schema = StructType([

# PATTERN 1: Automatic Broadcast Pattern
# =============================================================================
def automatic_broadcast_pattern(orders_df, customers_df):
    """
    Automatic Broadcast Pattern:
    - Spark automatically broadcasts small tables based on autoBroadcastJoinThreshold
    - No explicit broadcast hint needed
    - Works when table size < threshold (default 10MB)
    
    Use Case: Simple joins where dimension tables are small
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 1: Automatic Broadcast Pattern")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Spark automatically detects small table and broadcasts it
    result = orders_df.join(
        customers_df,
        on="customer_id",
        how="inner"
    )
    
    # Show execution plan - look for BroadcastHashJoin
    print("\nExecution Plan (Automatic Broadcast):")
    result.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    # Aggregate results
    summary = result.groupBy("customer_name", "tier") \
        .agg(
            count("order_id").alias("total_orders"),
            sum("amount").alias("total_revenue"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_order_value")
        ) \
        .orderBy(desc("total_revenue"))
    
    print("\nResults:")
    summary.show(10)
    
    return result

# =============================================================================
def manual_broadcast_pattern(orders_df, customers_df):
    """
    Manual Broadcast Pattern:
    - Explicitly force broadcasting using broadcast() function
    - Overrides automatic threshold checks
    - Useful when you know the table should be broadcast regardless of size
    
    Use Case: When you have domain knowledge about data distribution
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 2: Manual Broadcast Pattern")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Explicitly broadcast the smaller table
    result = orders_df.join(
        broadcast(customers_df),  # Force broadcast
        on="customer_id",
        how="inner"
    )
    
    print("\nExecution Plan (Manual Broadcast):")
    result.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    # Complex aggregation with window functions
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(desc("amount"))
    
    enriched_result = result.withColumn(
        "order_rank",
        row_number().over(window_spec)
    ).withColumn(
        "running_total",
        sum("amount").over(window_spec.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow))
    )
    
    print("\nTop Orders per Customer:")
    enriched_result.filter(col("order_rank") <= 3).show(15)
    
    return result

def conditional_broadcast_pattern(orders_df, customers_df, products_df):
    """
    Conditional Broadcast Pattern:
    - Decide whether to broadcast based on runtime conditions
    - Check table size or row count before broadcasting
    - Implement fallback strategies
    
    Use Case: Dynamic data scenarios where table sizes vary
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 3: Conditional Broadcast Pattern")
    print("="*80)
    
    def should_broadcast(df, max_size_mb=10, max_rows=100000):
        """
        Determine if a DataFrame should be broadcast based on conditions
        """
        # Get approximate size (this is an estimation)
        row_count = df.count()
        
        # Calculate approximate size in MB
        # Note: This is simplified; actual size depends on data types and compression
        sample_size = df.limit(100).cache()
        sample_size.count()  # Materialize
        
        # Decision logic
        should_bc = row_count < max_rows
        
        print(f"  Row Count: {row_count}")
        print(f"  Should Broadcast: {should_bc}")
        
        return should_bc
    
    # Check each dimension table
    print("\nEvaluating Customers Table:")
    broadcast_customers = should_broadcast(customers_df, max_rows=1000)
    
    print("\nEvaluating Products Table:")
    broadcast_products = should_broadcast(products_df, max_rows=5000)
    
    # Conditional join with customers
    if broadcast_customers:
        print("\nUsing Broadcast Join for Customers")
        result = orders_df.join(
            broadcast(customers_df),
            on="customer_id",
            how="inner"
        )
    else:
        print("\nUsing Sort-Merge Join for Customers")
        result = orders_df.join(
            customers_df,
            on="customer_id",
            how="inner"
        )
    
    print("\nExecution Plan:")
    result.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    # Calculate customer lifetime value
    ltv_result = result.groupBy("customer_id", "customer_name", "tier") \
        .agg(
            count("order_id").alias("total_orders"),
            sum("amount").alias("lifetime_value"),
            min("order_date").alias("first_order"),
            max("order_date").alias("last_order")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "customer_segment",
            when(col("lifetime_value") > 100000, "VIP")
            .when(col("lifetime_value") > 50000, "High Value")
            .when(col("lifetime_value") > 20000, "Medium Value")
            .otherwise("Low Value")
        )
    
    print("\nCustomer Lifetime Value Analysis:")
    ltv_result.orderBy(desc("lifetime_value")).show(10)
    
    return result
